articles.title: Ukraine's missile gap — Kyiv's struggle to close the ballistic divide
articles.body:
Ukraine's race for its own ballistic missile
Screenshot from a video showing a test launch of the FP-7 ballistic missile, published on Feb. 27, 2026. (Denys Shtilierman / X)
Incredibly fast and destructive, ballistic missiles have become a key feature of Russia's continuing long-range assault against Ukrainian cities. And while Kyiv has built world-leading drone technology, when it comes to producing ballistic missiles, a key capability in modern warfare, Ukraine still decisively lags behind Russia.
This could soon change, as Kyiv seeks to close the gap by mass-producing its own ballistic missiles, two of which are scheduled to enter service in the coming months.
Fire Point's new FP-7 short-range ballistic missile is due to enter service with the Ukrainian military within "weeks," with the longer-ranged FP-9 "currently undergoing flight tests," according to Fire Point's CEO, Iryna Terekh, speaking at a defense conference in Poland on Sept. 10.
"Ukraine’s new ballistic missiles could have a significant impact on the outcome of the war if they enter service in meaningful numbers," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
A battle of ballistics
Hoffmann said a ballistic missiles would give Ukraine the ability to quickly launch devastating missile strikes against valuable, time-sensitive military targets, such as Russian ballistic missile launchers — a capability Ukraine currently lacks, though one it desperately needs.
Broadly speaking, ballistic missiles fly in high arcs at hypersonic speeds and only a handful of air defense systems can intercept them. Cruise missiles fly significantly slower and lower to the ground, and are generally easier to intercept.
Ukraine relies on American-made Patriot PAC-3 air defense systems to defend itself against ballistic missiles and a chronic shortage of Patriot interceptors has left cities highly vulnerable ahead of winter.
Russia currently produces the munitions at a rate of "about 120 ballistic missiles every month."
Russia currently produces the munitions at a rate of "about 120 ballistic missiles every month", Ukrainian President Zelensky told a NATO-Ukraine Council meeting in Kyiv on June 3, a tempo of production that allows for sustained and deadly missile barrages against Ukrainian cities.
Unfortunately for Ukraine, Russian production of ballistic missiles far outpaces Western production of Patriot ballistic missile interceptors — which Lockheed Martin currently produces at a rate of around 50 per month — let alone Ukraine's ability to acquire the costly and in-demand missiles.
When Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, Ukraine possessed around 500 OTR-21 Tochka short-range ballistic missiles for around 90 launchers, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), with no ability to produce more. These Soviet-legacy missiles were both limited by range of a maximum of 120 kilometers (75 miles) and were relatively inaccurate compared to modern precision weapons.
In comparison, Russia fielded 900 modern and longer-ranged Iskander-M ballistic missiles in February 2022, according to the IISS, along with significant numbers of Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles, 3M22 Zircon quasiballistic missiles, and a large number of S-300 and S-400 surface-to-air missiles with a secondary land attack role.
By ramping up domestic production, as well as by sourcing supplies of munitions from North Korea, Russia has been able to maintain a stockpile of ballistic missiles while routinely subjecting Ukrainian cities to mass barrages.
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) assessed that by mid-2026, Russian stockpiles still held 130 Iskander ballistic missiles, 400 RM-48U ballistic missiles for the S-400 system, 120 Zircon quasiballistic missiles, 50 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles, and 50 North Korean ballistic missiles of various types.
In comparison, Ukraine currently has little to no serial domestic ballistic missile production. While President Zelensky claimed Ukraine had "begun using" the 1KR1 Sapsan short-range ballistic missile on Dec. 9, 2025, evidence of it entering widespread production has remained elusive. If the weapon system had indeed entered Ukrainian service, it did so in extremely small numbers.

Limited supplies
With such limited domestic production, Ukraine has relied on foreign allies for an extremely limited supply of replacement ballistic missiles — the American-made ATACMS. Ukraine officially received its first consignment of these older American missiles in October 2023. Unofficial reports suggested Ukraine received between 40 to 50 of the missiles.
Upon arrival, Ukraine immediately put them to use. On Oct. 17, 2023, Ukraine used M39 ATACMS to strike two helicopter forward operating bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdyansk, destroying 14 Russian helicopters, according to a British Defence Intelligence assessment — including eight Ka-52 attack helicopters — approximately 11% of Russia's entire fleet of that type.
Ukraine had to use its small stockpile of ATACMS sparingly, as opportunities to replenish stocks were extremely limited. The most significant replenishment came in August 2026, when Ukraine signed an agreement to purchase 70 M39 ATACMS missiles from Turkey as part of a wider arms deal.
This reliance on external supply from often unreliable foreign partners has created a key strategic vulnerability Ukraine has sought to address with domestic ballistic missile production. As part of this, leading Ukrainian defense company Fire Point spent 150 million euros to construct a solid rocket fuel plant in Denmark to support the development of Ukraine's new FP-7 and FP-9 missiles.
Ukraine's ballistic hopefuls
Fire Point has become an important domestic defense manufacturer since its founding in 2022, manufacturing a series of highly effective long-range drones, yet corruption allegations and questions about the ultimate ownership of the company have accompanied its rise.
Despite the allegations, Fire Point's FP-1 long-range drone has become a key part of Ukraine's deep strike campaign, while the FP-2 medium-range drone — which sacrifices range for a larger warhead — has become a mainstay of Ukraine's increasingly successful mid-range strike campaign.
"The development of Ukraine's drone program has demonstrated that, with sufficient funding and prioritization, significant results can be achieved in the production of long-range weapons," Nazarii Barchuk, an analyst at the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, told the Kyiv Independent, while noting that "ballistic missiles are a more complex type of weapon to manufacture."
Barchuk believes the critical factor will be ensuring "adequate funding for the program," including investment from foreign partners, as well as the "preservation and expansion of component production chains."
Although Ukraine's various domestic long-range drone programs have matured into a successful capability that frequently inflicts severe damage on Russian military and economic infrastructure, they have been less able to deal with more mobile military targets. Russian forces have frequently mitigated the damage of Ukrainian drone raids against military airfields by flying valuable aircraft away from incoming slow-flying drones.
read also
A learning curve
Fire Point also manufactures the FP-5 Flamingo heavy cruise missile, and while the first few operational uses saw the missiles fall short of their intended targets, recent Flamingo launches have been far more successful. In June 2026, three of the large cruise missiles struck the Titan-Barrikady manufacturing plant in Volgograd, damaging the facility.
"The Flamingo was fairly inaccurate in the beginning," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that Fire Point has since modified and upgraded its missile.
"The FP-5 Flamingo is now operationally more useful and I could see the same process taking place with the FP-7 and the FP-9," Hoffmann said.
The new FP-7 ballistic missile is designed with a claimed range of 200 kilometers (124 miles), a top speed of 1,500 meters per second (3,355 mph), and a 150-kilogram warhead. The missile is based on the Soviet-era 48N6 interceptor used in the S-300 and S-400 air defense systems, but uses modern components and manufacturing techniques.
"This will be an analog of ATACMS, probably even with a larger warhead. But it will cost at least twice as little," Denys Shtilerman, chief designer and co-founder of Fire Point, said in an interview in March. Shtilerman emphasized the goal was to produce the system en masse. "If you produce two or three ballistic missiles a month, it makes no sense. It will not affect the front," he said.
read also
Likely targets
"There will be different targets for each type of missile," Barchuk told the Kyiv Independent. "The FP-7 is designed for targets at the front line and in the immediate rear, such as headquarters and command posts, weapons storage facilities, military equipment (radar stations, electronic warfare systems, air defense systems, and missile launchers), drone launch sites and military infrastructure, including airfields within the missile’s range," he said.
The larger and more complex FP-9 is due to enter service "by the end of the year," according to Terekh.
The FP-9 is a significantly larger, faster, and longer-ranged missile, with a range of 855 kilometers (531 miles), a top speed of 2,200 meters per second (4,920 mph), and the ability to carry an 800-kilogram warhead.
Besides enabling strikes on a huge number of military facilities and important industrial sites, the missile also puts Moscow, as well as other Russian cities, within range.
"If Ukraine is able to mass produce around 50 FP-9 missiles per month, and if they're reasonably accurate so they can go after high-value military assets, as well as larger infrastructure targets, then it's going to get much more uncomfortable for the Russians," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent. "That would be really significant, I would say, but we have to get there first."
"The FP-9 has a longer range and a larger warhead," Barchuk said. "This missile is intended to strike targets deep in the rear, specifically on Russian territory. Their targets may vary, but priority is likely to be given to military-industrial facilities, protected weapons arsenals, critical communications nodes (including satellite communications), military installations and airfields from which Russian tactical aircraft take off to carry out strikes against Ukraine," he said.
The successful introduction of the FP-9 could be a significant upgrade of Ukraine's capabilities, Hoffmann said. "Within minutes you could strike, 600, 700, 800 kilometers deep into Russia, which could make ballistic missile launcher hunting or air defense suppression and destruction a lot more successful."

articles.title: ‘A Way for Russian Occupiers Go Home’: Ukraine Intel Reveals Why Kerch Bridge Still Stands
articles.body:
The bridge that Russian President Vladimir Putin built to cement Russia’s grip on occupied Crimea remains a powerful symbol of Moscow’s occupation. But as Ukraine intensifies its campaign to isolate Russian-occupied Crimea, striking railways, roads, ports, fuel facilities and other logistics nodes across the peninsula, one of the most recognizable symbols of Moscow’s occupation remains intact.
Why?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Major General Vadym Skibitsky, deputy chief of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR), offered a rare explanation during a panel discussion at the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference this week.
According to Skibitsky, the answer is partly practical: the Kerch Bridge is simply no longer as important to Russia’s military supply logistics as it once was.
“It’s really not so strategic an object for the Russian Federation today,” Skibitsky said.Ukraine has already destroyed or disrupted numerous other logistics routes across occupied Crimea, he pointed out, while Russia has increasingly shifted the movement of military supplies toward the land corridor running through occupied southern Ukraine.
Most military cargo, including weapons destined for Russian forces fighting in Ukraine now moves through Russia’s Rostov region and then along the so-called land bridge through occupied Ukrainian territory, according to Skibitsky.
Political weight
Despite the logistical shift, the Kerch Bridge has long been one of the most politically and strategically significant pieces of infrastructure linking Russia with the Ukrainian peninsula it illegally annexed in 2014.
UN Warns Ukraine Faces Toughest Wartime Winter Yet
“For Russia, for Putin, the Kerch Bridge is a symbol of the occupation of Crimea,” Skibitsky emphasized.
With that in mind, he offered another reason for keeping it standing – with a pointed message to Russian forces on the peninsula.
“It’s maybe one of the ways for Russian occupiers to return home.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, damaging it in major attacks in 2022 and 2023 and again targeting the crossing in subsequent operations. But Ukraine’s strategy toward Crimea has increasingly expanded beyond the bridge itself.
Skibitsky also recalled that the bridge had previously been a focal point of Western fears of escalation. He noted that several years ago, during discussions around Ukrainian operations against the crossing, some European countries raised concerns that destroying it could provoke a major Russian escalation, including nuclear threats.
Today, however, HUR assesses that the bridge’s military significance has diminished. The discussion over the Kerch Bridge led directly to a broader question: whether Vladimir Putin could actually use nuclear weapons if Russia faced a major military setback.
Any Russian use of nuclear weapons, including tactical nuclear weapons, would have consequences extending far beyond Ukraine and could reshape security calculations in other regions of the world, he said.
For that reason, Russia’s nuclear rhetoric remains a tool of pressure, but the Kremlin also has to consider the international consequences of crossing that threshold.
Missiles, drones and the wider threat
Skibitsky then outlined what HUR considers one of Ukraine’s most immediate military threats: Russia’s expanding missile and drone campaign.
“It’s not a risk, it’s a real threat,” he said.
According to HUR’s assessment, Russia’s defense industry plans to produce at least 100 ballistic missiles in September. Russia is also using North Korean ballistic missiles against Ukraine, Skibitsky said.
Asked how Ukraine could counter the threat, he described a multi-layered strategy. The first element is obtaining more interceptor missiles from Ukraine’s partners. The second is striking the factories and enterprises producing Russian ballistic missiles.
“We absolutely know all enterprises, factories, companies that are involved in the production of such ballistic missiles on the territory of Russia,” Skibitsky said.
The third is attacking the launchers themselves. According to Skibitsky, Russia can deploy between 17 and 19 ballistic missile launchers in regions including Kursk and Voronezh for strikes targeting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.
And the fourth element is sanctions – particularly restrictions preventing Russia from obtaining foreign navigation systems and electronic components needed for its weapons industry.
Skibitsky also addressed cooperation between Russian and Chinese companies supporting Russia’s industrial capabilities. HUR, he said, is aware of enterprises involved in joint production with Chinese companies. But many are located more than 2,000 kilometers from Ukraine, making them difficult to reach even with Ukraine’s expanding deep-strike capabilities. That makes international sanctions particularly important, Skibitsky said.
He pointed to problems Russia has encountered obtaining Chinese-made jet engines for certain unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) programs as evidence that pressure on supply chains can work.
Another unusual part of the discussion centered on Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon. Asked why facilities apparently associated with civilian businesses were being targeted, Skibitsky said HUR does not consider every such site purely civilian.
“Wildberries and Ozon and other such centers in the Russian Federation are really involved in the logistics system of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation,” he said.
According to Skibitsky, disrupting these networks is part of a much broader Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s military logistics. Ukraine first focused on logistics in occupied Crimea and other occupied territories, seeking to break supply routes supporting Russian forces in the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson directions.
The campaign has since expanded as Kyiv attempts to identify and strike the wider logistics infrastructure sustaining Russia’s war.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Kyiv-Warsaw train struck by Russian drone near Polish border as mass attack targets western Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Kyiv-Warsaw train struck by Russian drone near Polish border as mass attack targets western Ukraine
Key developments on Sept. 12-13:
- Russian drone hits Kyiv-Warsaw train near Polish border
- Russian drones target Volyn, Rivne oblasts in rare mass attack in western Ukraine
- Russian strikes hit 2 major Ukrainian steel plants, killing 2 and injuring 6
- Russian attacks kill 11, injure 96 across Ukraine as Odesa comes under mass overnight strike
- Ukrainian naval drone destroys Russian unmanned boat in Black Sea, Navy says
A Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw train near Ukraine's border with Poland, Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) reported. The train was about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border. No passengers were injured.
"This is (Vladimir) Putin's terror, 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Katerina Sergatskova, an award-winning journalist and entrepreneur who witnessed the attack, told the Kyiv Independent that Russian drones struck a gas station and a train locomotive near the Yahodyn border checkpoint on the Ukrainian-Polish border.
Following the attack, she and other passengers were left standing outside for several hours.
"We were told to evacuate immediately, but there was no shelter," Sergatskova said. "We were simply told to move away from the train cars toward the lake."
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least six civilians and injured 43 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Sept. 13, as Moscow launched a mass drone assault that heavily targeted western regions far from the front line.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 453 Shahed and Gerbera drones, including some jet-powered Shaheds, as well as Parodiya decoy drones and S8000 Banderol missiles.
Ukrainian forces intercepted 405 drones and six S8000 Banderol missiles. Hits were recorded at 13 locations, while falling debris was reported at seven other sites.

Russian drones target Volyn, Rivne oblasts in rare mass attack in western Ukraine
Russian forces launched a mass drone attack on western Ukraine on Sept. 12, injuring at least five people in Volyn Oblast and causing power outages in neighboring Rivne Oblast, regional authorities said.
Both regions are located in Ukraine's northwest, far from the front lines, making them less frequent targets for Russian attacks.
The attack on Volyn Oblast lasted more than four hours, with more than 10 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles entering the region’s airspace, according to regional Governor Roman Romaniuk.
Most of the drones targeted the Kovel community, Romaniuk said. Five people were injured and received medical assistance. No deaths were reported.
Debris from one of the drones also struck a passenger train in Lutsk. Passengers had been evacuated before the impact, and no one aboard was injured, according to the governor.
In neighboring Rivne Oblast, Russian attacks caused power outages in parts of Dubno and in the Rivne district, according to regional Governor Oleksandr Koval. An unspecified enterprise in the Sarny district was also destroyed in the attack.
No casualties were reported, and energy crews were working to restore electricity, Koval said.
The attacks illustrate Russia's ability to strike deep into western Ukraine, far from the line of contact. Volyn borders Poland and Belarus, while Rivne lies immediately to its east.
Western Ukrainian regions have repeatedly come under long-range Russian drone and missile attacks targeting energy, transport, and other infrastructure. While these regions are targeted less frequently than Kyiv or Odesa — and far less frequently than front-line cities in Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts — they have increasingly been reached by Russian drones during large-scale nationwide attacks.
On Sept. 3, Russian drones hit several western regions during a nationwide attack that killed five people and injured dozens.
The attacks on Volyn and Rivne were part of a wider Russian drone assault across Ukraine on Sept. 12. According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia launched nearly 500 strike drones at the country during the day.
"In essence, the Russians have expanded this war from the front lines, where they cannot achieve success, into the economic sphere, and their tactics are extremely primitive: to destroy every object that can help people endure the conditions of the war," Zelensky said.

Russian strikes hit 2 major Ukrainian steel plants, killing 2 and injuring 6
Russian missile strikes hit two major Ukrainian metallurgical plants overnight on Sept. 12, killing two people and injuring six others, according to statements from Zaporizhstal operator Metinvest and ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih.
In Zaporizhzhia, four ballistic missiles struck the Zaporizhstal steel plant, injuring four employees and causing what Metinvest described as critical damage.
The attack was the third ballistic missile strike on the plant in a month, following earlier attacks on Aug. 11 and Aug. 27. Zaporizhstal had still not resumed production following the previous strikes, according to Metinvest.
"Zaporizhstal produced pig iron and steel for civilian needs. The plant did not manufacture products for military purposes and did not host anything on its territory that could make it a military target," Metinvest Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko said.
"Even this did not stop another attack," he added.
The strike damaged equipment in the plant's blast furnace and open-hearth shops, as well as its energy systems, internal networks, and logistics infrastructure, Metinvest said.
One of the four injured workers received treatment at the plant and declined hospitalization, while three others were taken to hospitals with moderate injuries.
"The scale of the destruction is increasing with every strike," Myronenko said. "It is not yet possible to fully assess it, but preliminarily we consider the damage critical."
Separately, a Russian missile strike hit the ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih steel plant, which is in the city of Kryvyi Rih in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, overnight — killing two employees of contractor companies and injuring two plant workers, the company said.
Production and auxiliary facilities were damaged, while search and rescue operations continued at the site. The company said specialists were assessing the extent of the damage and possible timelines for recovery.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih noted that the facility is a civilian mining and metallurgical enterprise.
The plant has been hit repeatedly during Russia's full-scale war. A December 2022 strike killed one employee and destroyed a rolling mill, while another attack in August 2026 killed two plant employees and one contractor and injured 18 others, damaging key energy and blast-furnace facilities and partially halting production.
The attacks on the two plants were part of a broader wave of Russian strikes across Ukraine overnight on Sept. 12 that killed at least 11 people and injured 96 others. Odesa Oblast was the main target of the overnight missile and drone attack, while deadly strikes were also reported in Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, and Kharkiv oblasts, among others.

Russian attacks kill 11, injure 96 across Ukraine as Odesa comes under mass overnight strike
At least 11 people were killed and 96 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Moscow launched a mass overnight missile and drone attack targeting Odesa Oblast, local authorities said on Sept. 12.
In Odesa Oblast, at least 35 people were injured, including a five-month-old infant and a 17-year-old, local Governor Oleh Kiper said.
"The enemy attacked the city. A multi-story residential building was damaged," Kiper said as the first consequences of the strike emerged.
Russia launched 129 attack drones of various types overnight, including Shahed-type and jet-powered drones, as well as eight Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided missiles, and Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Ukrainian forces shot down 110 targets, with hits recorded at 20 locations and debris from intercepted targets falling at four additional sites.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, two people were killed and at least 22 others injured, including a child, local Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Dnipro, one person was killed and 19 injured as Russian drones, artillery, and aerial bombs damaged an enterprise, apartment buildings, garages, and vehicles.
Overnight, another person was killed and three injured in Kryvyi Rih after Russian forces struck an industrial enterprise. A 54-year-old man was hospitalized in serious condition, Hanzha added.
In Donetsk Oblast, four people were killed and five injured in Russian attacks over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Two people were killed in Sloviansk, while one person was killed in Kramatorsk and another in Yasnohirka.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed and 11 injured in Russian attacks, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 1,001 strikes against 45 settlements in the region over the past day, including five missile strikes on the city of Zaporizhzhia, according to Fedorov.
In Kyiv Oblast, one person was killed and three others injured, including a child, as Russian strike drones hit five districts over the past day, local authorities said. Damage was recorded in the Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil, and Vyshhorod districts. Fifteen sites were damaged, including seven homes, vehicles, warehouses, hangars, and a power line.
In Sumy Oblast, a 68-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone strike on the Myropillia community, while a 64-year-old man was injured in a separate drone attack on the Novoslobidska community, local authorities said. Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks against 25 settlements in Sumy Oblast over the past day, using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other unmanned aircraft, and guided aerial bombs.
In Kharkiv Oblast, a 32-year-old man was killed in an attack on Kharkiv, while a 19-year-old man was injured elsewhere in the region, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and seven other settlements using guided aerial bombs and multiple types of drones.
In Kherson Oblast, 18 people were injured in Russian attacks targeting residential areas as well as critical and social infrastructure, local authorities said. Fifteen apartment buildings were damaged, along with shops, a gas station, a service station, an ambulance, and vehicles.
Russian Shahed-type drones also struck railway infrastructure in Lutsk, Volyn Oblast, and Fastiv in Kyiv Oblast, Ukrzaliznytsia said. No passengers were injured after monitoring teams detected the threat in time and evacuated them, according to the state railway operator.

Ukrainian naval drone destroys Russian unmanned boat in Black Sea, Navy says
A Ukrainian unmanned surface vessel destroyed a Russian naval drone in the Black Sea in what Ukraine's Navy described as the "first-ever naval battle" between unmanned boats.
The operation was carried out jointly with Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), whose units detected the unmanned Russian vessel, the Navy said on Sept. 12.
The Russian drone was destroyed by a Ukrainian Sargan-3000 unmanned boat, equipped with a 12.7-mm Protector remote weapons station, according to the Navy. The drone-on-drone encounter marked a historic first.
"This is the first-ever battle between unmanned naval boats," the Navy said.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the Navy's report at the time of publication.
The joint operation represents a shift from naval drones attacking conventional ships to drone-on-drone maritime combat. Both Ukraine and Russia are increasingly moving toward unmanned warfare at sea.
Ukraine has dramatically expanded maritime-drone operations in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, hitting dozens of Russian vessels and maritime logistics targets this summer, striking 105 Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov campaign alone.
Russia is also developing and deploying more unmanned surface systems. Recent satellite imagery indicated Moscow was building what appeared to be its first dedicated naval-drone port in occupied Crimea.
Ukraine's Sargan-3000 is a naval unmanned system that passed combat testing in April 2026. The multi-purpose platform is "highly maneuverable" and capable of executing strike missions, according to the Navy.

articles.title: Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall
articles.body:
Ukraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.
Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.
This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it?
The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022, then left them to sink or swim. Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors and paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’s nauseating Alaska summit, and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price.
Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About 60% oppose ceding Donbas land to Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians also want it to stop. And like Moscow, Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch, notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly a deal to be done. But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away.
Efforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has now extended to the Red Sea (Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modern forever war phenomenon. Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but to win a Nobel peace prize (plus lucrative Russian energy deals).
Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas. Trump’s “board of peace” and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fear fighting will drag on indefinitely. Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together.
Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led to war crime atrocities such as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedly killed more than 100 schoolgirls in February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy.
Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightly restricted international journalists’ access to Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost of successful Iranian strikes on US bases in the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict.
Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now.
Western democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly, urged here) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war.

articles.title: Ansarallah widens Yemen’s western-coast gains despite Saudi airstrikes
articles.body:
Ansarallah widens Yemen’s western-coast gains despite Saudi airstrikes
TEHRAN — A massive ground offensive by the Yemeni Armed Forces just cleared Saudi-backed troops from 5,400 square kilometers of territory. Seven coalition military divisions dissolved in a matter of days.
Yemeni troops now hold the port of Mocha and the strategic Perim Island at the mouth of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The operation rolled through Taiz and Hodeidah under the banner “Allah Is Stronger in Might and More Severe in Punishment.”
Combat footage released on September 12 by Ansarallah documents a mechanized retreat. Yemeni fighters pushed heavy weapons through the Jabal Habashi ridges and ambushed fleeing coalition convoys.
Armor burned. Saudi drones fell from the sky. Inside the Khalid bin Walid School, which Saudi proxies occupied as a barracks, advancing units seized intact communications gear.
At the Jabal Tariq camp, retreating mercenaries left behind radar systems and vehicles. Hundreds of Saudi-aligned fighters surrendered.
Yemeni soldiers opened coastal prisons to free local detainees held for years.
Riyadh and Washington are reportedly trading blame. Citing anonymous sources, CNN reported that Saudi-backed battalions operated at barely 20 percent of their official strength.
Corrupt commanders padded payrolls with ghost soldiers. When the front lines broke, proxy units begged for air support.
U.S. Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper traveled to Saudi Arabia for urgent coordination talks, but the military cover Riyadh sought from Washington has not materialized.
After Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly appealed to President Donald Trump twice for U.S. strikes, Trump rejected the request, while Washington limited its support to intelligence and targeting assistance.
More than 100 U.S. military personnel reportedly remain stationed in Saudi Arabia providing targeting data. Their presence failed to stop the collapse.
Saudi Arabia responded to its ground defeat by bombing Yemen at least 129 times over the weekend. F-15 and Typhoon jets out of Khamis Mushait struck targets across seven provinces.
Sanaa retaliated immediately. Brigadier General Yahya Saree confirmed a heavy barrage of ballistic missiles and drones hit the Saudi military base in Sharurah. The strike bypassed U.S.-supplied air defenses to ignite fires in vehicle staging yards.
The battlefield squeeze is tightening. Yemeni infantry captured the heights of Jabal al-Rawa on September 13. Losing this elevation cuts the main supply route for thousands of proxy fighters in Taiz.
They now face a bleak choice. They can abandon heavy equipment and flee on foot through narrow valleys, or surrender.

articles.title: The arithmetic of US decline
articles.body:
The arithmetic of US decline
TEHRAN — The myth of American military omnipotence is dying not on a grand battlefield but in the quiet statistics of empty warehouses and the weary eyes of exhausted sailors. The United States projects an image of infinite power, yet closer inspection reveals a superpower suffocating under the weight of its own hubris. The numbers are devastating. The strategic calculus is broken. For the Islamic Republic, the path to regional dominance is now paved with the debris of American logistical failures.
Consider the missile arsenal. Before the current conflicts, Washington boasted roughly 2,300 Patriot Advanced Capability interceptors. Today, CSIS puts the remaining stock at about one third. America is down to its last 36 percent of Patriot missiles, a reality forcing its allies to the back of the line. The Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system functions at barely half capacity, with stockpiles between 52 and 62 percent. The Precision Strike Missile, hyped as the future of American long-range fires, is effectively nonexistent, with stocks down to 10 to 22 percent.
This is not a supply chain hiccup but an industrial failure of epic proportions. Even the Tomahawk cruise missile holds at roughly two thirds of its prewar stockpile. That scarcity explains why Japan’s order for 400 missiles has been delayed and why the acting Navy secretary confirmed a freeze on sales to Taiwan. Representative Michael McCaul, who signs off on foreign arms sales, admitted that when Washington cannot deliver, it hurts alliances because the promise cannot be kept. But admission does not solve the arithmetic. If American defense industry can produce 600 interceptors a year, rebuilding the pile takes four years, assuming no one fires another shot. Wars do not pause for factory schedules.
The math against current reality is fatal. In a single night, during a single strike on a single base, Jordanian forces reportedly fired enough interceptors to stop 18 of 20 incoming missiles. That was one base on one night in a war where Iran has already launched more than 1,500 ballistic missiles. The consumption rate renders American stockpiles useless within weeks. Pentagon planners know this. They are trapped in a cycle of depletion that their economic base cannot sustain. The United States cannot outproduce the resolve of the Axis of Resistance.
While arsenals dwindle, the human machinery of empire is grinding to a halt. For months, the Pentagon paraded the USS Abraham Lincoln as the crowning jewel of American might. Yet the carrier’s recent deployment told a story of exhaustion. After 286 consecutive days at sea, a record the Western press breathlessly celebrated, the Lincoln limped into Pattaya, Thailand, for what was essentially a morale rescue. Five thousand sailors and Marines disembarked into a port where Thai authorities braced for incidents involving American personnel. When American families and even their own lawmakers raise concerns about deployment lengths, it reveals a military machine running on fumes. The stopover was not a victory lap but an admission of human limitation.
The United States can project force, but it cannot project endurance. The Lincoln’s extended deployment consumed fuel, parts, and psychological resilience that America cannot indefinitely replenish. When a carrier strike group’s port call becomes a liability rather than a strategic maneuver, the empire is running on empty.
The deepest humiliation came beneath the waves. The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps executed a flawless operation near the Strait of Hormuz, capturing an intact American unmanned underwater vehicle, the Anduril Dive LD. This is not scrap metal. The Dive LD is a sophisticated autonomous system, measuring nearly six meters, capable of operating for 10 days at depths of 6,000 meters. Its modular design allows intelligence gathering, mine warfare, and seabed mapping. Now it sits in Iranian hands, a treasure trove of physical architecture, sensor arrays, and propulsion secrets.
Washington pretends reverse engineering is impossible, but they know better. Even partial analysis of this machine gives the Islamic Republic an unprecedented window into American autonomous warfare. The United States sent its most sophisticated underwater spy into waters Iran has studied and dominated for decades. The spy came home in an Iranian net. That is the bitter truth of asymmetric warfare: every tool of aggression becomes a source of intelligence when captured intact. The humiliation is not that American technology failed. It is that technological superiority cannot guarantee strategic success.
Geography remains the eternal enemy of empire. The Strait of Hormuz sits beside Iranian territory, a chokepoint we control with layered defenses of missiles, drones, mines, and coastal artillery. America may possess global reach, but reach is not control. The United States cannot sustain its presence against Iranian resistance. The carrier exposes the burden of endurance. The captured drone exposes the vulnerability of technology. The empty missile warehouses expose the bankruptcy of strategy. For Washington, the lesson is inescapable: global military reach is not unlimited power. In today’s security environment, especially in the Persian Gulf, outcomes depend on what a military can sustain, protect, and convert into durable political results.
The United States is a paper tiger, capable of impressive parades but unable to translate technological superiority into strategic victory. Each round of this conflict leaves Iran stronger, holding the chokepoints, absorbing the technology of its enemies, and watching the American war machine suffocate on its own logistics. The superpower is bleeding out, not from a single blow, but from a thousand cuts delivered by geography, economics, and the unyielding will of a determined nation. The math is done. Washington has lost.
The question is no longer whether Washington can project power into the region. It can. The question is whether it can sustain that power long enough to impose its will. That is the question Iran has forced America to answer and the answer is becoming increasingly uncomfortable.
Washington still has the missiles, the carriers and the money. But it is discovering that none of them guarantees endurance. Iran has turned geography into a weapon, time into an advantage and American consumption into a strategic vulnerability. That is the real arithmetic of decline: Washington has the arsenal, but Tehran holds the map.

articles.title: Russia Faces Shortage of Chinese Drone Jet Engines
articles.body:
Russia is experiencing operational disruptions in obtaining Chinese-manufactured jet engines for its long-range strike drones following coordinated diplomatic and intelligence interventions by Ukraine and its international partners, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
Speaking at the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) conference in Kyiv, Deputy Head of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) Vadym Skibitsky underscored the critical necessity of expanding multilateral sanctions targeting supply chains that sustain Moscow’s aerial bombardment capabilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“That is why I emphasize once again: international sanctions are needed. Today, the Russian Federation has certain problems with jet engines for drones. We are talking about engines from China. This is the result of our actions and the actions of our partners,” Skibitsky stated.
The intelligence official noted that Beijing is acutely aware of the regulatory and economic risks facing its domestic industrial sector if it deepens its commercial and logistical entanglement with Russia’s wartime defense industry.
Skibitsky added that Ukrainian military intelligence has mapped the full network of Russian enterprises and joint production ventures operating alongside Chinese suppliers. However, he cautioned that targeting these installations directly remains an operational challenge due to geographic depth.
“Unfortunately, they are located far from our border – at a distance of over 2,000 kilometers. Hitting such targets is not easy. This is possible only with long-range strike assets, particularly unmanned aerial vehicles,” Skibitsky explained.
Drones Target Nizhnekamsk Hub and Slavyansk Refinery in Russia
Manufacturing bottlenecks
In recent weeks, the Russian military has increasingly relied on turbojet-powered loitering munitions and hybrid drone-missiles as its primary aerial strike vector against Ukrainian urban centers and critical infrastructure.
The primary platforms deployed include the Geran-4 and lower-cost “Banderol” loitering munitions.
Despite their heavy operational deployment, Ukrainian technical analysts indicate that Moscow is grappling with inventory constraints.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian presidency on defense technology, stated that Russian forces currently lack sufficient stockpiles of jet-powered Shaheds to stage the mass saturation raids seen earlier in the war, when hundreds of propeller-driven drones were launched simultaneously.
Instead, Beskrestnov noted that the Russian military is fielding newly produced jet drones literally straight off the assembly line to sustain continuous pressure against Ukrainian air defenses.
Air defense challenges posed by turbojet systems
The deployment of turbojet engines represents a major evolution from earlier propeller-driven Shahed models powered by internal combustion engines.
Equipped with miniature aircraft-grade turbine engines, the newer drones operate at altitudes of several kilometers and achieve speeds between 400 and 600 kilometers per hour, nearly three times faster than piston-engine variants.
Their increased velocity and cruising altitude allow them to outpace Ukraine’s primary fleet of propeller-driven anti-drone interceptors, effectively functioning in an air defense profile more comparable to low-altitude cruise missiles.
While Ukrainian air defenses routinely intercept over 90% of slower Shahed variants, interception rates for jet-powered drones have hovered near 60%, forcing the Ukrainian military to commit high-end surface-to-air missiles and combat aircraft to counter the threat.
Technical teardowns of captured munitions have repeatedly identified Chinese-sourced components within the guidance and propulsion systems of Russian drones.
Chinese manufacturers – such as Shenzhen-based Telefly Telecommunications Equipment – have supplied microturbine engines and electronic sub-assemblies to Russian defense contractors.
Although Western sanctions have targeted shell companies and intermediaries facilitating component transfers through Hong Kong and third countries, Ukrainian defense officials have reiterated that throttling the flow of foreign turbine engines remains pivotal to containing Russian long-range aerial assaults.

articles.title: Drones Target Nizhnekamsk Hub and Slavyansk Refinery in Russia
articles.body:
Drones targeted the major petrochemical and oil refining cluster of Nizhnekamsk in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan and sparked a fire at an oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, Krasnodar Krai.
In Nizhnekamsk, situated roughly 1,200 kilometers from the Ukrainian frontier, residents reported low-flying unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overhead followed by a series of heavy blasts and anti-aircraft artillery fire near the industrial district, according to independent Russian outlet Astra and Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russia’s Unified State System for Prevention and Elimination of Emergency Situations (RSChS) issued regional drone alerts across Tatarstan overnight.
Local officials acknowledged an incident within the industrial zone, with regional official Radmir Belyaev confirming an ignition “at one of the city’s enterprises,” widely reported by monitoring groups to be Tatneft’s TANECO refining complex.
Nizhnekamsk houses one of the Russian Federation’s most critical fuel and chemical manufacturing hubs. The complex includes Tatneft’s TANECO facility, ranked among Russia’s five largest oil refineries with an annual crude processing capacity exceeding 16 million metric tons, alongside the adjacent TAIF-NK refinery, which processes more than 7 million tons of crude petroleum and gas condensate annually.
The industrial hub also hosts Nizhnekamskneftekhim, a Sibur subsidiary and one of Europe’s largest synthetic rubber and polymer producers, which holds a dominant domestic market share in synthetic rubber and industrial plastics utilized across civilian and defense manufacturing sectors.
Ukraine Tests Automated Drone Warning System for Gas Stations
Fire ignites at Slavyansk-on-Kuban refinery
Concurrently, overnight drone attacks struck the Slavyansk-on-Kuban oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar Krai, triggering a blaze at the facility, Astra reported.
Geolocated video footage published by local residents on social media showed a large fire and an orange glow illuminating the night sky above the plant. Regional authorities have not released an official assessment of the structural damage or casualties.
The Slavyansk refinery, operated by Slavyansk ECO, has an annual processing capacity of approximately 4 million tons of crude oil. The facility had previously halted processing operations following Ukrainian drone strikes in late April and June that caused fires in the plant’s atmospheric distillation units.
Subsequently, the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (HUR) confirmed that operators from the Department of Active Operations and the Department of Unmanned Systems of the Main Intelligence Directorate, as part of a joint deep-strike operation with the Ukrainian Defense Forces, struck the “Slavyansk-ECO” oil refinery in the city of Slov ’yansk-on-Kuban in the Krasnodar Krai.
“As a result of the operation, a key oil refining facility and the company’s tank farm – which fuel the criminal war against Ukraine – were struck,” HUR stated.
Thick smoke and the glow from the major fire at the Russian oil refinery are visible from dozens of kilometers away.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine also reported that units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the “Slavyansky” oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, Krasnodar Krai, and the “Taneco” oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, Republic of Tatarstan, as well as command posts and storage facilities for the Russian invaders’ attack drones.
Expanding campaign against Russian energy and chemical sectors
The overnight strikes in Tatarstan and Krasnodar Krai follow an intensified campaign by Ukrainian forces against Russian defense manufacturing, fuel distribution networks, and chemical plants over the weekend.
On Saturday, Sept. 12, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukrainian forces struck two major chemical industry enterprises in Russia’s Samara and Perm regions, alongside targets in the Black Sea and occupied territories.
In the Samara region, overnight drone strikes on Saturday ignited a blaze at the KuibyshevAzot chemical facility in Tolyatti, which produces roughly 50% of Russia’s caprolactam and 75% of its industrial tire cord.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine subsequently confirmed a direct strike on the nearby Tolyattikauchuk plant, which produces synthetic rubbers, monomers, and high-octane gasoline additives essential for manufacturing solid rocket fuel used in tactical and ballistic missiles.
In the Perm region, long-range drones targeted the Azot plant in Berezniki on Friday, Sept. 11, which manufactures nitric acid and ammonium nitrate – critical industrial precursors for military-grade explosives.
Simultaneously, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) conducted an operation against five military and logistics installations in Taganrog, Rostov region, striking a first-person-view (FPV) drone production workshop, two UAV warehouses, an oil storage tank, a P-18 radar station, and a Pantsir-S2 air defense system.
Ukrainian long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries over 70 times since early 2026, significantly reducing domestic fuel output and compelling at least 17 Russian regions to introduce fuel sales rationing.

articles.title: Iran requested new Russian Geran drones for attacks on Israeli, American targets amid war - report
articles.body:
Tehran requested that Russia provide the regime with its new generation of Geran drones earlier this year during the Israeli-US war with Iran, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.
The report cited Western security officials and a source close to the Kremlin, who said that Iran made the request following substantial improvements to Russia's Geran family of drones.
According to the report, the jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5, which follow their propeller-powered predecessors, have recently entered the Ukraine-Russia war and pose a much greater threat than earlier generations because they can evade defenses more easily.
Geran drones based on Moscow-produced Iranian Shahed design
Russia based the original Geran on Iranian-designed Shahed drones, which Moscow began producing in 2023.
The first-generation Geran carries a 20-kilogram warhead and has a top speed of 185 kph, while the new Geran-5 carries a 90-kilogram warhead at a top speed of 600 kph.
According to the Financial Times, it looks more like a cruise missile than a traditional Shahed drone. In contrast, the Geran-4 is less revolutionary but is more aerodynamic than its predecessor. Both have longer ranges than previous generations.
Both models also include thermal vision, AI-powered targeting, Russian anti-jamming antennas, and Chinese mesh radio network modems, while older designs relied on rudimentary guidance systems, the report added.
The report also cited pro-Kremlin media as saying the Geran-5, in particular, can be deployed by Russian Sukhoi-25 fighter jets, aircraft Tehran purchased in 2025.
In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of supplying Iran with Shahed drones to use against the US and Israel, telling CNN's Fareed Zakaria that it is "100% facts" that Iran has used Russian-made Shaheds to attack US bases.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukraine drone strikes kill four as Russia attacks close to Poland border
articles.body:
Ukraine drone strikes kill four as Russia attacks close to Poland border
Russia says four people killed in Ukrainian strikes as both sides continue to attack each other with waves of drones.
Several civilians have been killed and more than 20 others wounded overnight as Russia and Ukraine continue to attack each other with waves of drones to try to shift momentum in the more than four-year-long war.
Russia launched 863 drones at Ukraine over the last 24 hours, the Ukrainian General Staff said on Sunday.
Russian forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night, the country’s Ministry of Defence said, including over Tatarstan, other Russian regions, and the occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Russia carried out two drone attacks near Ukraine’s border with NATO member Poland, Polish and Ukrainian officials said.
The Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack on a truck about 0.8km (0.5 miles) from Poland, but the crossing has since resumed operations, Polish border guards told the Reuters news agency on Sunday.
Warsaw and Kyiv also said a Russian drone struck a Warsaw-bound train near the Polish border in Ukraine but caused no casualties.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its forces had struck Ukrainian logistics and energy facilities overnight. They also targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in western Ukraine, it said. Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.
In Odesa, at least nine people were injured in a Russian night-time attack, according to Serhiy Lysak, who heads the city’s military administration.
Odesa is home to Ukraine’s main port hub on the Black Sea and has for months faced sustained drone and missile strikes, with Kyiv accusing Moscow of trying to choke off its exports.
Meanwhile, the head of Russia’s Rosatom nuclear corporation, Alexey Likhachev, said two people were killed in a series of drone strikes which targeted fuel trucks near the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
Separately, authorities in Russia’s Tatarstan region said two people were killed and 12 others were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk.
‘We don’t rule out talks’
Later on Sunday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said three-way negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the United States could take place in October, Russian media reported.
“We do not rule out such a possibility; we are talking about the foreseeable future,” RIA Novosti and TASS news agencies reported, quoting Peskov.
US negotiators have recently visited Kyiv and Moscow in a bid to ramp up negotiations to end the war, while US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, have held talks over the phone.
In an interview aired on Saturday, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami, US, in December for talks.
Several previous attempts at negotiations involving the US have failed.

articles.title: Poland responds to Russian attacks on western Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland responds to Russian attacks on western Ukraine
Poland’s Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk made the statement on X, according to Ukrinform.
“Anyone wondering whether Ukraine should be supported militarily should draw conclusions from this night,” Tomczyk wrote.
He said that for many people, the war “may still seem like something distant and almost surreal, but in reality, it is happening very close to the Polish border.”
“Today’s attacks show this very clearly,” the Deputy Defense Minister stressed.
According to Tomczyk, in a single night, Russia launches hundreds and sometimes nearly a thousand aerial attack weapons at Ukraine – ballistic and cruise missiles, guided aerial bombs and drones. Some of them head westward.
“Every missile destroyed and every drone shot down is a threat that does not fly any farther,” Tomczyk stressed.
He noted that the Polish Air Force operates almost every night in the airspace over the Lublin and Podkarpackie voivodeships.
Tomczyk stressed that Ukraine’s victory in the war is in the interests of Poland and all of Europe.
“Russia is waging a terrorist war, and Putin bears responsibility for it. The sooner this war ends, the better it will be for the security of our region,” he said.
At the same time, Poland’s Deputy Defense Minister emphasized that “there will be no lasting peace without a strong Ukraine and without the unity of states that understand what the Russian threat means today.”
Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also commented on Russia’s overnight attack on Ukraine.
“Before dawn, our systems detected an attack by several Geran-5 jet-powered drones in western Ukraine. One of them struck one kilometer from the Polish border, another five kilometers away,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote.
According to him, during the attack, Polish airspace was monitored by F-16 fighter jets, helicopters and a Saab airborne reconnaissance aircraft. No violation of Polish airspace was recorded.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said Russian forces are “changing their attack tactics, increasingly using jet-powered drones, launching several at a time and thereby exhausting Ukrainian air defenses.”
The official stressed that Poland’s air defense remains on constant alert.
As reported by Ukrinform, overnight on September 13, a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing on the Polish border was damaged in a Russian attack on Ukraine’s Volyn region.
In addition, Russian forces attacked the locomotive of a passenger train two kilometers from the Polish border.
In Poland, an air raid alert was issued in the Lublin and Podkarpackie voivodeships in response to the Russian attack on Ukraine, and Polish fighter jets were scrambled. Processing of documents at Polish-Ukrainian border crossings was also temporarily suspended.

articles.title: Ukraine Reportedly Opens New Drone Front Against Russia in Africa
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Ukraine Reportedly Opens New Drone Front Against Russia in Africa
Ukraine is expanding its use of drone warfare beyond Europe, deploying specialists to Africa to support forces confronting Russian troops and Moscow-linked military structures.
Around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are currently operating in Mali, helping local forces counter Russia’s Africa Corps through training, technical support, and operational planning, CNN reported on September 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian team works closely with the Azawad Liberation Front, a predominantly Tuareg rebel group active in northern Mali. Rather than taking part in frontline combat directly, the Ukrainian specialists assist local fighters with planning and conducting drone operations.
One Ukrainian drone operator told CNN that he coordinates local fighters remotely. “I coordinate their operations remotely. The signal from their drone comes to me via the internet, and I immediately tell them by radio what to do and where to fly,” he said.
According to CNN, the operator receives live drone footage over the internet and relays instructions to local pilots by radio. He said Ukrainian personnel have been ordered not to deploy directly to frontline positions.
Ukraine expands drone operations across Africa
CNN reported that Ukrainian specialists have also operated in Sudan, while personnel from Chad, Niger, and Burkina Faso have traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian instructors.
The missions are part of a broader effort by Kyiv to apply expertise developed during Russia’s full-scale invasion in other regions where Moscow is expanding its military presence.
Ukrainian teams have also traveled to at least five countries in the Middle East, according to CNN, where they trained local forces to counter Iranian-made Shahed attack drones, which Russia has repeatedly used against Ukraine.
In exchange for Ukrainian technical expertise, Kyiv has received security cooperation agreements and commitments involving ammunition supplies, CNN reported. The deployments also allow Ukrainian specialists to test equipment and tactics in environments significantly different from the Ukrainian battlefield.
In Mali, daytime temperatures regularly exceed 43 degrees Celsius, while dust and sand accelerate wear on drones, electronics, cooling systems, filters, and batteries. A Ukrainian intelligence representative told CNN that the tactical environment is also markedly different.
“In Ukraine, it is high intensity, massed strikes, constant pressure. Here, it is more maneuver warfare across large areas, ambushes, control of routes, work by small groups and dependence on knowledge of the terrain,” the source said.
According to CNN, Ukrainian personnel teach local fighters how to use drones while learning desert survival and combat techniques from forces familiar with the Sahel.
Ukraine targets Russia’s position in Mali
Ukrainian personnel also described operations around Kidal, a strategically important city in northern Mali.
Earlier in 2026, Tuareg rebels and militants launched attacks against Russian forces in the area. Moscow later accused Kyiv of involvement and claimed Ukrainian and European instructors had helped prepare local forces for the operation.
CNN cited a Ukrainian intelligence source as saying that Kyiv views such missions as a way to increase pressure on Moscow and weaken Russia’s image as a reliable security partner in Africa. “We are turning our experience in drones into a foreign policy tool,” the source said.
Russia has significantly expanded its military presence across the Sahel following the withdrawal of French and other Western forces from several countries in the region.
After the Wagner Group was dismantled, Moscow transferred parts of its African operations into the Defense Ministry-controlled Africa Corps, which supports governments aligned with the Kremlin and helps protect Russian strategic and economic interests.
Ukrainian naval drone teams reportedly operate in Libya
Ukraine’s activities in Africa also extend to Libya, CNN reported. According to the outlet, Ukrainian naval drone operators are active in northwestern Libya and have used a base in Misrata to support operations against vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
The fleet consists of tankers used to transport Russian oil and reduce the impact of international sanctions, providing Moscow with continued export revenues.
CNN reported that one explosive-laden Ukrainian naval drone involved in such an operation later moved beyond the control of its operators and appeared near the Greek island of Lefkada. Greece issued a diplomatic protest, after which Kyiv formally apologized, according to the report.
The reported missions in Mali and Libya show how Ukraine is increasingly using drone expertise developed during the war against Russia to contest Moscow’s military and economic activity outside Europe.
“It puts pressure on them. This whole story has both psychological and real consequences,” a Ukrainian operator told CNN.
Russia, meanwhile, continues expanding its military footprint in Africa as it seeks political influence, access to natural resources, and strategic positions in countries where Western involvement has declined.
The reported missions come months after Ukraine unveiled its first comprehensive strategy to expand its presence and influence across Africa. In March, Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov said Kyiv aimed to strengthen its political, economic, and security role on the continent and more actively defend Ukrainian interests there.
