articles.title: Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
articles.body:
Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
A global surge in diesel prices is being driven by the Russia-Ukraine war, the US president says.
United States President Donald Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure, saying they were to blame for a global fuel shortage that was driving up prices, and not the war with Iran.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said on Sunday, speaking to reporters during a trip to the Republic of Ireland. “We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel. That’s hurting the world.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Saudi Arabia shuts critical oil pipeline after drone attack: What it means
- list 2 of 3Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes
- list 3 of 3Iran and Ukraine wars: Why ship fuel is running short, and why it matters
A wave of long-distance Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in recent months has reduced that country’s fuel production, triggering petrol shortages across the country.
Ukraine, which faces regular Russian attacks on its own energy infrastructure, says refineries are legitimate military targets. Kyiv says Russia’s oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow’s more-than-four-year-old invasion of its neighbour.
Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in midterm US elections in November.
The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the US on Friday, reaching a national average of $6.06 a gallon ($1.60 per litre) according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily prices. The price of diesel a year ago, according to AAA, was $3.71 a gallon ($0.98 per litre).
The fuel has a significant impact on the cost of transportation, and is used by ships, trains, and trucks to move international goods, many of which are now more expensive, as those costs are passed on to consumers.
On Sunday, Trump said the increase in the price of diesel “isn’t done by the Middle East, this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine”.
Oil prices globally have gone up since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in February, disrupting the flow of oil from the region, including through the Strait of Hormuz, and causing a global energy crisis. Around one-fifth of the world’s oil passes through the strait in peacetime.
Crude oil prices crossed the $100-per-barrel mark last week for the first time since July. Brent crude, the global benchmark, climbed as high as $109 at one point.
The war in Ukraine is, along with the Iran conflict, having an impact on diesel prices too, according to the International Energy Agency.
A monthly report from the agency published on September 11 said the war between the US and Iran was hampering efforts to normalise flow through the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, but the Russia-Ukraine conflict also was having an influence, particularly on diesel supplies.
“The disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the agency said.

articles.title: Israeli troops in Syria call for 'conquest of Damascus'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli troops call for 'conquest of Damascus' amid continued attacks on Syrian territory
Israeli reservists have called for the military to expand its illegal operations deeper into Syrian territory, with a senior officer saying many troops would favour advancing as far as Damascus, according to Israeli media.
Reserve officers serving with the Israeli army's 210th Division have criticised limits on the scope of its operations in southern Syria and called for increased activity inside Syrian villages and surrounding areas, Israeli news site Walla reported.
The officers reportedly argued that deeper incursions would help push what Israel considers potential threats further away from its border.
A senior Israeli officer defended the military's current approach but acknowledged the appetite among reservists for a more wide-scale invasion of Syria.
"Would the reservists like to conquer Damascus? Many of them would," Walla quoted the officer as saying.
The issue was also raised during a visit by Israeli military chief of staff Eyal Zamir around two weeks ago, according to the report.
The officer said reservists deployed to Syria often arrived after serving in Gaza and Lebanon, where the operational environment was significantly different.
"What is happening today in Syria is beyond anything we imagined and any activity we thought of - the activity is non-stop," he said.
Israel currently operates from 10 military positions inside Syrian territory, according to Walla, conducting operations around the clock based on intelligence and military assessments.
The report said Israeli forces have conducted raids well beyond the immediate border area, singling out Beit Jinn in the western Damascus countryside, around 11 kilometres from the occupied Golan Heights.
The senior officer said some reservists wanted to reach Beit Jinn "every day", saying that 14 militants had been killed in three separate Israeli raids in the area.
The comments come amid continuing Israeli military operations around Beit Jinn and elsewhere in southern Syria.
Israeli forces carried out a series of incursions in the Damascus and Quneitra countrysides on Saturday, sources told The New Arab.
An Israeli force comprising two tanks, a bulldozer and more than 10 other vehicles entered agricultural land surrounding the Beit Jinn farm area in the western Damascus countryside, according to the sources.
Another force of three military vehicles entered an area west of Saida al-Hanout in the Quneitra countryside, while four Israeli military vehicles entered the town of al-Rafid, where soldiers searched several homes.
Israeli forces also fired an artillery shell at agricultural land in the Ain al-Shaara area near Beit Jinn following similar shelling overnight.
Israeli military operations have become increasingly frequent in southern Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime in December 2024.
Israel moved troops into the UN-patrolled buffer zone separating the two countries following Assad's fall and has since established military positions and carried out raids, arrests and strikes deeper inside Syrian territory.
Syria and the United Nations have said Israel's deployment violates Syrian sovereignty and the 1974 Disengagement Agreement governing the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces.
France on Friday called for Israeli troops to withdraw from Syrian territory, while reiterating its support for efforts to reach a security agreement between Damascus and Israel.
The French foreign ministry told Syria's official SANA news agency that any military deployment within the separation zone constitutes a violation of the 1974 agreement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has condemned Israel's violations of Syrian sovereignty, saying Damascus had received support from more than 40 countries at the UN Security Council.
He reaffirmed Syria's territorial integrity and said it would continue defending its rights through "all legitimate political and diplomatic means".
A UN commission investigating Syria said earlier this week that Israeli military activity in the country's south had become "increasingly sustained and entrenched", warning that some Israeli actions could amount to war crimes.

Part of workshop destroyed: OSINT analysts reveal damage to Russian chemical plant from Flamingo missile strike
OSINT analysts from the Exilenova+ community have released satellite imagery showing the consequences of a strike on a Russian speciality chemicals plant in Volgograd. A Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile destroyed part of a workshop at the facility.
Source: Exilenova+; Fire Point, Flamingo's manufacturer
Details: Exilenova+ explained that Ukraine's defence forces struck the Volgogradpromproekt plant on the night of 10-11 September. A missile hit the plant's main workshop.
"One of the FP-5 missiles completely destroyed a 20x15-m section of the main workshop," Exilenova+ stated.
The use of the Flamingo missile was confirmed by its manufacturer Fire Point. According to the company, the FP-5 completely destroyed an annex building.
"As a result of the strike, a building covering approximately 380 sq m completely collapsed and was destroyed," the company said.
Meanwhile, the OSINT analysts reported that one of the missiles did not reach the plant. A crater from a Flamingo strike was recorded near the facility in Volgograd.
The Volgogradpromproekt plant specialises in speciality chemicals, producing organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants, resins and other chemical components for industry. Its products are used in Russia's aviation and shipbuilding industries and the defence industrial base.
The plant produces ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts and develops chemical production technologies.
Background: On the night of 11-12 September, Ukraine's defence forces attacked the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara Oblast. The plant supplies Russia's military-industrial complex.

articles.title: Europe should impose sanctions after every massive Russian strike, not wait for packages – Sybiha
articles.body:
Europe should impose sanctions after every massive Russian strike, not wait for packages – Sybiha
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this at a joint briefing with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski in Kyiv on Sunday, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"We discussed once again the approach that we should not wait for large sanctions packages, but after every massive strike on Ukraine, adopt relevant sanctions packages against the aggressor – against Russia – including an 'Anti-Ballistic Package'," he said.
Sybiha added that Ukraine's partners should deprive Russia of its ability to manufacture ballistic missiles and drones and restrict its access to military technologies. According to him, there is still significant potential in this area.
"Unfortunately, Russia has learned how to circumvent sanctions. Unfortunately, Russia continues to use components of products manufactured in Western countries, in European countries, in the production of both ballistic missiles and drones. And we have provided this information to our European partners," the diplomat said.
As reported, a bill to strengthen sanctions against Russia, which the U.S. Senate approved by an overwhelming majority last month, will be put to a vote in the House of Representatives next week.

articles.title: Making Iraq ‘normal’ again: do mass arrests and cash seizures signal end to corruption?
articles.body:
The gates of the Green Zone in Baghdad are made of five-metre-high armoured steel, reinforced with horizontal girders, and strung between concrete pillars and anti-blast walls. Police water cannon trucks are stationed nearby, along with armoured personnel carriers and squads of heavily armed soldiers.
At the first sign of street protests – over failing electricity, unemployment or, more recently, the US-Israeli attacks on Iran – the gates are shut. X-shaped vehicle barriers, made from welded iron beams and mounted on wheels, sit ready at the roadside alongside coils of razor wire; both are slid across the street, sealing off the sprawling neighbourhood, home to the presidential palace, parliament, the prime minister’s office, the massive fortress-like US embassy, and other institutions, including the homes of scores of politicians and members of parliament.
When the gates are closed, traffic is diverted, creating monumental jams lasting for hours for most Baghdadis who lack the coveted Green Zone badges.
In the early hours of 28 June, the gates were shut, US-made Abrams tanks prowled through the streets, and black-clad counter-terrorism units fanned out across the area. Only this time, the measures were meant to prevent those inside from leaving, rather than to keep those outside from getting in.
By dawn, Iraqis woke to the news that nearly 50 people, including a dozen MPs and senior officials, had been detained, along with the seizure of hundreds of millions of dollars in cash and gold. Pictures and videos, purporting to show masked officers hauling out safes full of money, piles of jewellery and suitcases filled with dollars, circulated widely.
The arrests were met with the greatest Iraqi schadenfreude since the beginning of time. For if Iraqis – of all persuasions, sects, ethnicities and social backgrounds – agree on one thing, it is the rottenness and corruption of the political parties that have held power since 2003, and the greed of a clique of party bosses, businessmen and militia leaders.
‘Not just something every PM does’
On the day of his inauguration as Iraq’s new prime minister in early May, Ali al-Zaidi, a 41-year-old with a round face, thin beard and sharp eyes, delivered, in stilted language riddled with grammatical mistakes, the standard repertoire of promises made by every prime minister before him, Iraq’s own version of making the country great again: supporting local industry, agriculture and youth; fixing the electricity supply and solving the housing crisis. But the two issues the wealthy businessman with little political experience emphasised as most urgent were disarming the pro-Iranian factions and fighting corruption “with no red lines”.
With Iraq’s coffers nearly empty after the near-total halt of its oil exports since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, these two issues – militias and corruption – are interlinked and, in the shadow of war, are threatening the state itself.
But the prime minister before him, and the one before that, had both begun their tenures with similar gestures – declaring the exposure of vast corruption networks – and both had ended their time in office mired in corruption charges of their own, while the country’s public services remained in ruins. So why should this time be different?
“No, this isn’t just something every prime minister does,” a government insider told the Guardian. “No, this is unprecedented – a real earthquake inside political circles, because it’s a signal to all the politicians about what could happen to them. To everyone, without exception.”
What we are seeing, he said, is a prime minister trying to dismantle the financial empires of the political parties – empires built on corruption that is naked and clear for all to see, and that implicates every single politician without exception. “So when you pick four or five of them and strike,” he said, “you are sending a message to everyone: what happened to those people can happen to all of you, if you don’t do such and such.”
Division of the spoils
Al-Zaidi came to power as a compromise candidate after months of negotiations among the Coordination Framework, the bloc of major Shia parties and figures in parliament, and after the Trump administration vetoed the leading candidates.
The negotiations – really a haggling over the division of spoils – are a well-rehearsed exercise, repeated after every election for the past two decades, under a system known as muhasasa, which has become the cornerstone of Iraqi politics, devised by Iraqi opposition parties in exile in the 1990s as a power-sharing arrangement that would prevent Iraq from again sliding into a dictatorship. The arrangement was imported wholesale after the 2003 US invasion by those same parties and the Americans; under muhasasa, the prime minister is a Shia, the president a Kurd. But muhasasa also came to mean the division of government posts among all the political factions: Sunni, Shia, Kurdish and others.
Party bosses and militia commanders feud, threaten and cajole, some claiming to represent the historical rights of their community, others decrying the historical injustices imposed on theirs, all in an attempt to increase their share of the lucrative ministries and state institutions, turning them into party fiefdoms, running every possible scheme to defraud the treasury.
“The parties have built states within the state,” an international banker, who was hired by a previous government to help clean up the system, said. “We probably have seven or eight of these mini-states, siphoning between 5% and 10% of every government contract.”
The stooge?
In the muhasasa power-sharing system, if the minister of oil is Shia, at least one of his deputies – and it is always “his” – will be Sunni.
Here a second round of haggling and horse-trading begins within the Sunni blocs and parties over the lucrative post. It usually comes down to a kind of exchange rate – how many directors of education, health and culture is one deputy oil minister worth?
Once a party has won the post, the contest shifts to finding the right candidate. Sometimes the parties bring in someone from within their own ranks, ideologically committed to them, or a relative of the party boss. But in most cases, they choose someone from the bureaucracy instead – someone familiar with the running of the state, versed in the rules and regulations of an archaic and dysfunctional system: mandarins who have succeeded in weaponising these often-conflicting regulations accumulated over more than a century, from the Ottomans, to the British who imported a system for the Indian Raj, to the military dictators who added a socialist flavour, and finally the young American zealots who arrived in Baghdad after the 2003 war that toppled Saddam Hussein and wanted to create a neoliberal free market state, without any knowledge of Iraq or its history.
The regulations are deployed at every level to obstruct every state function – from the issuing of an ID card to the signing of a multibillion-dollar contract – until a bribe is paid to ensure the task’s smooth completion.
In January 2025, Adnan al-Jumaili – a young engineer with a pleasant, smiling, square face, lean, with a trim moustache and thick, prematurely greying hair – was appointed deputy oil minister responsible for refineries.
His fast rise through the ranks, first as director of a single refinery, then as director of the state institution overseeing the northern refineries, responsible for several plants, was celebrated in some pro-government local press as the placement of a young, honourable and efficient talent at the helm, one who would end years of mismanagement and setbacks.
He appears in several videos alongside the then prime minister, Mohammed Shia al-Sudani, who had been chosen by the same Shia parties to lead a government focused on delivering essential services.In video after video, al-Sudani is shown with his chest puffed out, wearing black sunglasses, cutting ribbons to inaugurate projects and showcase his government’s achievements, while beside him, a smiling al-Jumaili, in a hi-vis vest and helmet, briefs him on the details. In one clip, he even receives an “honourable employee” award from al-Sudani.
But soon after al-Sudani lost his bid for a second term and al-Zaidi became prime minister, it all came crashing down.
Al-Jumaili was the first to be arrested, on 30 May, and arraigned on television in a yellow jumpsuit, surrounded by dozens of machine guns and boxes of ammunition found at his home. Investigators said they had also recovered $10m (£7.4m) in cash, 3bn dinars (about $2m) and 1.5kg of gold, along with around 40 properties across Baghdad and other provinces. In the weeks that followed, more wealth surfaced: cash stuffed into plastic water bottles, hidden down a rainwater drain, concealed in walls – and, allegedly, 7bn Iraqi dinars that his wife was caught trying to burn in an outdoor oven. By mid-July, the total seized in the case had reached 127bn dinars ($96m) and $24m in cash, plus properties, vehicles and 375kg of gold, and 70 properties as well as a number of cars.
What shocked many Iraqis was the sheer vulgarity of it all – the way the money, the product of elaborate schemes devised to siphon millions, only for it to end up buried underground or stashed in boxes and large, family-size plastic pickle jars.
According to the judicial investigation, al-Jumaili ran a scheme that had yielded hundreds of millions of dollars.
In a meeting with Iraqi journalists the next day, al-Zaidi said that al-Jumaili had tried to bribe him before his arrest with $200m to keep his post – in some reports, the total offer was said to reach $600m.
Whether al-Jumaili was the mastermind of all the corruption, or whether it had been laid out for him in advance, is unknown. But from the moment he arrived at the ministry of oil, he began amassing huge commissions from contracts and awards handed to companies and contractors and from diverted shipments of fuel.
As last year’s elections neared, he became a conduit for delivering millions of dollars to candidates, many on the prime minister’s list, though not all.
One politician told the Guardian: “Many parties came in and benefited from working with al-Jumaili, and he regarded all of this as protection for himself.” As his connections to political parties expanded – not only to the Sunni bloc that had nominated him, but allegedly to his bosses at the ministry of oil and in the prime minister’s office – he came to believe he was untouchable. And as his political cover grew, he began to commit catastrophic mistakes, the politician said. “Because, you see, he was telling himself he was now beyond reach – that it was impossible for anyone to touch him.
“So he began making mistakes, overreaching – faking warehouse deliveries, for example, and diverting fuel to create phantom storage stock that didn’t exist. We started hearing about thousands of phantom day-labourers, whose wages were being paid out even though they didn’t exist in the first place. We heard about transport contracts inside the refineries worth millions of dollars – contracts at astronomical figures.”
“The Adnan al-Jumaili affair is, I think, a model of the way things are run, the way the process of placing people in particular positions works,” the government insider said. “These positions are responsible for generating large revenues, illegally, for a party or for several parties. It’s like bitcoin mining, you see, they generate money.”
Investigations into al-Jumaili’s financial dealings had begun the previous October, when the judiciary began looking into spending irregularities in the elections and discovered that he had funnelled money to numerous candidates. This eventually led to his arrest and, after his confessions, to the mass arrests on 28 June.
‘That chapter must close’
The investigations and arrests coincided with two things: severe pressure on Iraqi finances brought on by the war, and a more active role by the US in shaping Iraqi politics.
According to government insiders, members of parliament and a source close to the judiciary, the Americans – weary of dealing with Iraqi politicians continuously failing to achieve any reforms – had built a rapport instead with the Iraqi judiciary. The new American envoy, Tom Barrack, played an active role, encouraged by the judiciary’s increasingly assertive statements on the state’s monopoly of weapons.
For many months, investigators searched for a corruption case that could be exposed publicly. The challenge was finding one that, when exposed, would make headlines domestically and internationally, while guaranteeing that the fallout would not bring down the entire post-2003 political system. Al-Jumaili’s case was perfect: it implicated a number of prominent politicians, but stopped short of naming the big party bosses.
As one official put it: “You don’t know, in the end, if you keep pressing on these parties – what might the armed factions do? What might Iran do?” The case also touched a nerve sensitive to the Americans specifically: the smuggling of Iraqi oil.
“The government and judiciary are aiming to achieve two goals,” the government insider said. “The first is to recover as much as possible of the money that the parties and political leaders have siphoned over the years.” (In several statements, the prime minister has hinted that if the money is returned, there will be no further legal repercussions.) “The second is to sever, in all its forms and details, the relationship between the parties and the state – meaning the relationship between the economic offices of these parties and every corner of the state apparatus. In other words: the parties will no longer be able to extract anything from the state.
“The idea that the parties live off quotas they receive from the state – through projects, commissions and so forth – must come to an end. That chapter must close. And I believe this is the most important thing that could happen in Iraq’s modern history.”
It seems that bringing in al-Zaidi, or at least the support he is getting from the US and the judiciary, was calculated precisely for this moment, he and other officials said. Someone with sufficient experience and knowledge of the mechanisms involved in routing money out of the state, who knows how money is smuggled, channelled and extracted through contracts, projects, commissions and so forth.
Will this latest drive to fight corruption deliver any serious results? Or will it turn out to be, at best, another cosmetic operation – if not a case of political score-settling? And how can Iraq become a normal state, capable of reform, while it sits on a regional faultline, caught amid a multi-pronged war fought across its land and skies – and can that reform ever be achieved without accountability for the party bosses and the mini-states they’ve built?
“There are no guarantees that corruption will end, and that parties will stop looting the state,” the government insiders said. “But what we’re hearing is that there really is a governmental and judicial desire to end a certain phase and begin a new one – a situation where things are normal, where basic services are available, where this constant crisis over fuel, electricity, water and every other detail comes to an end. Where the situation becomes normal, meaning: our state becomes like any other state in the world, with its successes and its failures.”

Zelenskyy Says He Is Ready to Meet Putin at December G20 Summit in Miami
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he is prepared to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December and meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin there if Putin also takes part in the gathering.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In an interview with Deutsche Welle conducted on September 11 at the Canadian Forces Base North Bay, Zelenskyy said a face-to-face meeting should focus on reaching concrete decisions rather than exchanging statements.
“Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, talk and make decisions,” Zelenskyy said when asked whether he would be willing to meet Putin at the summit. The Ukrainian president added that the substance of any potential meeting would be measured by its outcome.
“It does not matter what I tell him or what he wants to tell me. Only the result will matter. That is all,” Zelenskyy said. The G20 leaders’ summit in Miami is scheduled for December 14-15, 2026. Ukraine is currently not listed among the invited non-G20 countries on the summit’s official website.
It also remains unclear whether Putin will attend the meeting in person.
Zelenskyy has previously said that Ukraine, the US, and Russia could hold a trilateral meeting as early as this autumn. He said he first plans to meet US President Donald Trump in September, after which work could begin on organizing broader negotiations.
The Ukrainian president has named Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United Arab Emirates among possible venues for future trilateral talks, saying other countries have also offered to host negotiations. He has indicated that issues including energy and grain could be discussed.
Zelenskyy and Putin have not held direct talks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Their only in-person meeting took place in Paris on December 9, 2019, during a Normandy Format summit involving Ukraine, Russia, France, and Germany. Zelenskyy and Putin held a brief bilateral meeting before wider negotiations between the Ukrainian and Russian delegations.
Earlier, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the possibility of a limited winter ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, potentially including a mutual pause on strikes against energy infrastructure.

Ukraine’s Armed Sea Drone Destroys Russian Drone in World’s First Naval Drone Battle
Ukraine’s Navy said it destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel in the Black Sea using an armed Ukrainian naval drone, describing the engagement as the first recorded battle in history between two uncrewed surface vessels.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The operation was conducted jointly by the Ukrainian Navy and Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR), according to a statement released by the Navy on September 12. Ukrainian intelligence units detected the Russian vessel before a Sargan-3000 naval drone was deployed to intercept it.
The Ukrainian drone was equipped with a remotely operated RWS Protector turret armed with a 12.7 mm machine gun.
“Ukraine’s Sargan destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel. The Navy, in cooperation with the Main Directorate of Intelligence, conducted a successful operation in the Black Sea and destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel. This is the first naval battle in history between uncrewed surface vessels,” the Ukrainian Navy said.
According to footage released by the Ukrainian Navy, the Sargan-3000 opened fire on the Russian vessel from a distance of approximately one kilometer.
The Russian vessel attempted to move away but was eventually immobilized and destroyed. The footage indicates that the Sargan operator targeted the vessel’s communications antennas early in the engagement, potentially disrupting its remote control.
The Russian uncrewed vessel sustained multiple hits before sinking. The Ukrainian Navy did not disclose the precise location of the engagement or provide details about the Russian vessel’s intended mission.
The Sargan-3000 is a Ukrainian-made multipurpose uncrewed surface vessel that was officially adopted by the Ukrainian Navy in April 2026. According to publicly available specifications cited by Ukrainian media, the platform has an operational range of up to 1,600 kilometers, can reach speeds of approximately 40 to 55 knots, and can carry a payload of up to 450 kilograms.
Earlier, in July 2026, Ukraine’s Navy said a Sargan-3000 sea drone sank the Russian FSB patrol ship Izumrud near Novorossiysk. The vessel had taken part in Russia’s 2018 attack on Ukrainian Navy boats in the Kerch Strait.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills 2 Palestinians in fresh Gaza violation
articles.body:
At least two Palestinians were killed and 13 other were wounded on Sunday in fresh Israeli airstrike on a vehicle in the Gaza Strip, medical staff said.
The strike in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood in western Gaza City, left the vehicle mangled, according to footage circulated on social media.
Witnesses told Turkish Anadolu Agency (AA) that the drone fired at least two missiles at the vehicle, killing its two occupants immediately and injuring nearby passersby.
Local medical staff told Reuters that they urged people to provide information that could help identify the two people who were killed and whose bodies were dismembered by the explosion.
The Israeli military claimed the strike targeted two Hamas members, without giving further information.
Separately, Israeli forces fired artillery shells toward Palestinian homes northeast of the Bureij refugee camp in central Gaza, according to local sources.
Israeli military vehicles also opened heavy fire toward buildings and tents housing displaced Palestinians in southern Khan Younis, while Israeli warships fired toward the city's coastline, witnesses said.
An October 2025, U.S.-backed cease-fire halted large-scale fighting in Gaza, but it has not ended Israeli strikes and there has been little progress on steps toward permanent peace.
Israel violates the cease-fire on daily basis and undermines efforts to implement U.S. President Donald Trump's broader plan to end the Gaza conflict, which includes the Israeli withdrawal from the strip and the disarmament of Hamas.
Israeli military has killed more than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, in Gaza since the cease-fire took effect, according to the territory's health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers died.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Hit Odesa High-Rise, Postal Depot, and Power Grid
articles.body:
Russian forces launched consecutive strikes against southern Ukraine late Saturday, Sept. 12 and early Sunday, Sept. 13, hitting a Nova Poshta postal depot and a residential high-rise in Odesa, while causing power outages across Mykolaiv.
In Odesa, Russian forces attacked the regional capital around midnight on Sunday, damaging a multi-story apartment building, Odesa City Military Administration Head Serhiy Lysak reported.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The enemy has attacked Odesa again. A multi-story building was damaged,” Lysak stated on Telegram, urging residents to remain in shelters as aerial threats continued.
The Ukrainian Air Force had issued warnings prior to the explosions, tracking Russian “Banderol” loitering munitions heading directly toward Odesa.
Earlier on Saturday evening, a Russian jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) struck a facility belonging to the postal and logistics company Nova Poshta in the Odesa region, injuring two people.
Odesa Regional Military Administration Head Oleh Kiper confirmed the strike on social media, publishing photographs showing damage to the logistics branch.
“As a result of an enemy strike by a jet-powered UAV, a branch of a logistics company was damaged. The facade of the building, glazing, and a cargo vehicle sustained damage. Two people were injured,” Kiper said.
Blackouts in Mykolaiv following power grid strike
Concurrently on Saturday evening, Russian forces attacked energy infrastructure in the neighboring southern city of Mykolaiv, causing blackouts across multiple city districts.
Russian Attack Halts US-Owned Oleina Sunflower Oil Plant in Dnipro
Acting Head of the Mykolaiv Regional Military Administration Heorhiy Reshetilov reported that municipal power networks sustained direct damage.
“In the evening, the enemy attacked Mykolaiv’s energy infrastructure. Several districts of the regional center have been partially de-energized,” Reshetilov stated.
Reshetilov added that utility emergency crews would begin power restoration work as soon as local security conditions permitted.
Consecutive bombardments across southern regions
The weekend strikes follow a major combined missile and drone bombardment targeting the Odesa region early Saturday morning, Sept. 12, that injured at least 35 civilians in the regional capital and damaged residential high-rises and energy pipelines.
During Saturday morning’s assault, fires engulfed the 21st through 23rd floors of a 25-story apartment building in Odesa, with emergency services rescuing 13 residents, including trapped occupants freed from elevators. Search-and-rescue teams later recovered the body of a deceased resident from the debris of the damaged structure.
In nearby Chornomorsk, Saturday’s strikes injured five people – including four children – and destroyed private residential properties and a hotel housing a rehabilitation facility.

articles.title: Zelenskyy sanctions former press secretary Mendel
articles.body:
Zelenskyy sanctions former press secretary Mendel
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has imposed sanctions on Yuliia Mendel, who previously served as his press secretary.
Source: presidential decree of 13 September
Details: Zelenskyy enacted a National Security and Defence Council decision on the imposition of personal sanctions against a number of individuals.
Among them is Yuliia Volodymyrivna Mendel, a 40-year-old Ukrainian citizen.
According to the president's website, Zelenskyy signed three decrees enacting National Security and Defence Council decisions to impose sanctions on vessels in Russia's shadow fleet, companies and individuals linked to the Russian state corporation Rostec, and propagandists who justify Russian aggression.
The sanctions target 20 maritime vessels that Russia uses to export oil, oil products and liquefied gas.
One of the decrees imposes sanctions on 29 Russian citizens and 29 Russian companies, including companies involved in supply chains for high-precision industrial equipment, electronics, and components used in missile and drone production. The restrictions also target companies producing dual-use goods, research organisations developing technical documentation for Russia's military-industrial complex, and an educational institution that trains specialised personnel for companies belonging to the Russian Kalashnikov concern. The sanctions also target companies that design solutions and supply high-tech equipment to Russian military-industrial complex companies, as well as IT companies that develop and maintain software for information encryption, data collection, and database management.
"Another decision imposes restrictions on 10 Russian and Ukrainian individuals who spread disinformation and Russian propaganda and support Russia's aggressive policy towards Ukraine. Yuliia Mendel is among those sanctioned," the president's website said.
Ukraine will transmit all the information to its partners for the synchronisation of sanctions in international jurisdictions.
Background:
- In May 2026, in an interview with notorious former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, Mendel claimed that the Ukrainian delegation at the Istanbul talks in spring 2022 was prepared to accept all of Russia's demands to end the war, citing only conversations with unnamed individuals. Among other things, Mendel accused Zelenskyy of money laundering and taking drugs in nightclubs.
- Mendel also claimed that Andrii Yermak, former head of the President's Office, performs magic rituals, including visiting cemeteries and using "dead water".
- She also described Yermak as "a very dangerous person" and said he makes her fear for her life. She spoke in very general terms, referring to "her experience" and "her contacts", but provided no details to substantiate her claims.

articles.title: Russian intelligence using fake volunteers to ‘hunt’ Ukrainian troops – SSU
articles.body:
Russian intelligence using fake volunteers to ‘hunt’ Ukrainian troops – SSU
SSU spokesperson Artem Dekhtiarenko said this during a television broadcast, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“We have also recently seen a trend whereby pseudo-volunteers approach military personnel. In other words, the enemy exploits any vulnerabilities that may exist in a serviceman’s psychological profile – this could be a desire for closeness, intimacy and so on. Or a Russian operative may simply approach someone and say: ‘I want to help you as a soldier in a difficult situation. I’m a volunteer, and we have humanitarian aid. Please tell me the address where we can send you a package.’ And instead of food and other supplies, a bomb arrives in that package,” he said.
Dekhtiarenko noted that another continuing trend involves Russians posing as journalists and contacting military personnel through their personal accounts, inviting them to interviews without coordinating with the press services of their respective military units.
“Either they conduct these interviews online and try to obtain sensitive service-related information, or they say: ‘Let’s meet at some location.’ And when the person arrives at that location, everything has already been prepared in terms of a bomb. So, please, remain vigilant,” the spokesperson said.
Asked which Russian institutions are involved in such activities, Dekhtiarenko said that virtually all of Russia’s intelligence and security services are operating against Ukraine, including the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces (GRU), and the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
“They can often carry out similar tasks. If we are talking about a network of bots, other Russian structures that use this method operate in much the same way. They cast a wide net and then work with whoever responds. For example, they send text messages to servicemen saying, ‘Hi, you’re handsome.’ In fact, such messages can be sent to a million service members, and then they respond to whoever engages with them,” the spokesperson explained.
As reported, the SSU has launched a new stage of a nationwide information campaign aimed at countering the recruitment of Ukrainians by Russian intelligence and security services.

articles.title: Germany Weighs Restricting NATO Defense Plans if AfD Governs
articles.body:
German defense officials are weighing procedural measures to bar regional administrations from accessing confidential national and NATO defense plans if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) enters government following state elections, Bloomberg reported.
The security contingency discussions were prompted by regional voting in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD secured 44% of the vote, capturing 39 of 83 seats in the state parliament and falling just three seats short of an outright majority.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius aims to ensure that any state administration led or influenced by the pro-Russian AfD would be legally and operationally prevented from accessing sensitive defense documentation that could be shared with Moscow.
At the center of the security review is Germany’s Operational Plan (OPLAN), a confidential, 1,000-page defense blueprint drafted by German authorities alongside NATO planners.
The document coordinates joint defense responses, military mobility, and emergency protocols between federal authorities and regional governments during a conventional military crisis or allied defense emergency.
According to an insider familiar with the discussions, Pistorius outlined the security initiatives during a closed-door consultation with defense policy experts from governing coalition parliamentary groups.
German defense planners operate under the working assumption that OPLAN protocols could be activated in the event of open escalation between NATO and Russia.
Budanov Eyes Trilateral Ukraine Peace Talks in October
Regional access controls
OPLAN relies heavily on Germany’s central geographic location within Europe, where the country functions as the primary logistical transit corridor and rear operational staging area for allied NATO forces advancing toward eastern positions during an Article 5 contingency.
Under standard operational protocols, the comprehensive version of OPLAN is provided directly to the heads of all 16 German federal states, while regional administrative bodies and interior ministries receive access to specific annexes and logistical chapters pertinent to their geographic territory.
Over recent months, German officials have debated legal and administrative mechanisms to safeguard military intelligence in the event that the AfD takes control of regional interior ministries or state police forces.
Proposals under review include redacting specific logistical chapters, compartmentalizing infrastructure data, or reclassifying regional transit schedules to restrict access exclusively to vetted federal personnel.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), classifies the AfD’s regional branches in Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, and Saxony as confirmed right-wing extremist entities deemed hostile to the country’s free democratic basic order.
Political fallout in Berlin
The debate over military intelligence arrives amid political reverberations across Berlin following the Saxony-Anhalt election, where the AfD achieved its strongest regional result to date. The governing Christian Democratic Union (CDU), led in the state by incumbent Minister-President Sven Schulze, dropped to roughly 18% of the vote.
The electoral triumph placed the AfD – led in the state by 35-year-old Ullrich Siegmund – within reach of attempting to assemble a governing cabinet. National co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla hailed the outcome as a historic turning point and a strategic template for federal parliamentary elections in 2029.
In Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced mounting internal party pressure over the scale of the defeat, with CDU employee wing chairman Dennis Radtke describing the result as a “watershed moment” that demands a fundamental reassessment of the party’s containment strategy.
Although the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority in Magdeburg, forming an alternative governing coalition remains mathematically fraught.
The traditional cross-party cordon sanitaire against the AfD would require complex negotiations among the CDU, Social Democrats (SPD), Greens, and the socialist Left Party, while the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could emerge as a potential kingmaker if it clears the 5% parliamentary threshold.

articles.title: UN Warns Ukraine Faces Toughest Wartime Winter Yet
articles.body:
Ukraine could face its most grueling winter since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 due to systematic and expanding aerial bombardments targeting civilian and energy infrastructure, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Administrator Alexander De Croo warned in an interview with the BBC.
Speaking to the broadcaster, De Croo said Ukraine is entering the cold season from a “very weak position” as Russian strikes continue to pound the power grid, fuel distribution networks, and commercial centers across the country.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This includes gas stations, shopping malls, and business centers, but above all, energy infrastructure, transmission lines, and similar assets. There is absolutely no justification for this,” De Croo stated, emphasizing that the UN remains deeply concerned about the potential humanitarian consequences as temperatures drop.
De Croo cautioned that extensive destruction of heating plants, electricity networks, and municipal utilities could disrupt water supply, heating systems, and sewage networks in sub-zero weather.
He noted that if temperatures drop toward -20 degrees Celsius, the compounding damage to municipal life-support systems would create conditions bordering on a humanitarian catastrophe.
The UN official described current recovery efforts as an urgent “race against time” to repair battered power plants and distribution substations before freezing weather sets in.
‘A Way for Russian Occupiers Go Home’: Ukraine Intel Reveals Why Kerch Bridge Still Stands
Through the UNDP, international agencies are assisting Ukrainian authorities in restoring damaged assets while accelerating the deployment of decentralized, smaller-scale energy generation units designed to be more resilient and less vulnerable to concentrated missile and drone strikes.
However, De Croo characterized maintaining and rebuilding the energy system under persistent Russian bombardment as an almost impossible task.
Repair crews must routinely operate during active air raid alerts, fully aware that the facilities they are fixing are prime military targets, frequently forcing emergency pauses in critical restoration work.
Domestic resilience plans and decentralization
The UN’s assessment follows statements by Ukrainian officials outlining domestic preparations to counter expected winter strikes.
Speaking at the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) forum in Kyiv, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi stated that while fully shielding every facility remains unfeasible, Ukraine is better prepared to withstand grid attacks than it was ahead of last winter.
Koretskyi noted that the government has formulated comprehensive resilience plans, with primary efforts directed toward decentralizing heating, water, and power infrastructure across municipalities to prevent regional grid collapses.
The prime minister acknowledged that Russian strikes have multiplied over the past two months, creating additional economic and logistical burdens, but affirmed that the state possesses the resources and technical reserves required to manage the heating season.
Ukraine met its baseline winter natural gas storage target a month early, accumulating 14.6 billion cubic meters in underground facilities by late August, according to First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal.
Concurrently, municipal utility crews had prepared approximately 100,000 residential buildings alongside 12,400 local boiler facilities and 11,700 kilometers of district heating pipelines by late August.
The Ukrainian government has allocated approximately Hr. 6.8 billion ($152 million) toward grid repairs, decentralized backup generators, and physical blast protections to ensure critical municipal services continue functioning during localized blackouts.

articles.title: Drone attack prompts Poland to evacuate more than 600 people from two border crossings with Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Drone attack prompts Poland to evacuate more than 600 people from two border crossings with Ukraine overnight
This was reported during an emergency meeting at the Polish Government Security Center, attended via video conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, by representatives of the Nadbużański Division of the Polish Border Guard, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
According to them, starting at 2:00 p.m. on Saturday, vehicle processing was periodically suspended on the Ukrainian side due to the threat of Russian drone attacks. Poland, in response to the situation in Ukraine, also suspended processing at its border crossing points.
Border guards noted that Ukraine had warned for several days in a row about the possible threat of attacks by Russian drones and had asked the Polish side to temporarily suspend processing at certain border crossing points.
Specifically, on September 10, there were three such requests regarding the “Dorohusk-Jagodzin” border crossing and two regarding the “Zosin–Ustyluh” border crossing. On September 11, the Ukrainian side requested once that processing be suspended at the “Dorohusk-Jagodzin” border crossing, and on September 12, twice at the “Dorohusk-Jagodzin” border crossing and twice at the “Zosin–Ustyluh” border crossing. According to Polish border guards, frequent warnings began to arrive following Russian attacks on Ukrainian border crossings on the border with Moldova.
Around 4 a.m. on Sunday, a Russian drone attacked a gas station approximately two kilometers from the “Dorohusk” border crossing. According to Polish border guards, the force of the explosion was such that “the windows in the Border Guard Service building rattled.” An evacuation of the border crossing was immediately ordered. Specifically, 25 Border Guard Service employees, 25 Customs and Tax Administration staff members, and more than 280 other people who were on the border crossing premises were evacuated. Among them were passengers from five buses. Service personnel took shelter in pre-designated shelters, while passengers and other people were led outside the checkpoint.
At approximately the same time, the Polish side received information about an unidentified object moving toward the “Hrebenne–Rava Ruska” checkpoint. A decision to evacuate was also made there. More than 300 people, including over 280 passengers, were evacuated from this border crossing point. Sixty-six employees of the Border Guard Service and the Customs and Tax Administration took shelter in designated safe areas. According to Polish border guards, after consulting with the military, it was determined that the threat of an imminent strike on the “Hrebenne” border crossing had not been confirmed.
At 8:27 a.m., the Polish side recorded another strike on a spur line in Ukraine. According to information received from Ukrainian authorities, a drone struck the locomotive of a freight train consisting of empty tank cars.
According to Polish authorities, following previous incidents at the border, procedures were developed to respond to the threat of drone attacks near border crossing points. In the event of an alert, passenger buses are moved outside the border crossing area, and personnel are directed to shelters. Polish border guards also noted the need to strengthen protection for personnel remaining along the state border, in particular by installing protective structures capable of providing cover while allowing them to monitor the border.
Special attention was paid during the meeting to vehicles transporting hazardous cargo, particularly fuel. As noted, due to long lines at border crossing points, these vehicles could pose an additional danger in the event of an attack.
On Sunday, near the “Dorohusk” border crossing, police and border guards had already begun moving vehicles carrying hazardous cargo further away. According to Polish authorities, these measures are intended to minimize risks to people in the event of possible drone attacks near the border.
As reported by Ukrinform, during an emergency meeting, Tusk stated that Poland must be prepared for increased Russian activity in the coming weeks and months, and that it cannot be ruled out that the escalation could also affect Polish territory.

articles.title: Russia admits it is striking 'everything and anything' in Ukraine
articles.body:
Moscow is now striking targets indiscriminately across Ukraine in response to Kyiv's intensified attacks on Russian territory, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Sept. 13.
Peskov claimed Russia had previously avoided indiscriminate strikes but changed its approach after Ukraine began targeting Russian economic and strategic infrastructure.
"The Russian Federation did not strike everything and anything," Peskov told reporters. "It started doing so after the Ukrainians themselves opened Pandora's box."
Peskov's remarks echoed Russian President Vladimir Putin's earlier warning that Ukraine had "opened Pandora's box" by striking Russian economic targets.
Putin said on Aug. 22 that Moscow would retaliate by targeting Ukraine's "sensitive economic sectors."
"(Ukraine) set out to damage our economy. What did it do? It opened this Pandora's box itself. Expect a response targeting your most sensitive economic sectors," Putin said in late August.
Moscow has dramatically increased the number of jet-powered attack drones it launches against Ukraine in recent weeks, with Kyiv facing particularly heavy and near-constant attacks.
Russian drones have targeted Kyiv almost continuously for more than a week, from late August into early September, leaving residents concerned about what the coming winter will bring.
Russia has systematically targeted Ukraine's energy grid since the first year of the full-scale war, inflicting extensive damage on critical infrastructure and causing repeated power outages.
Ukraine, in turn, has stepped up strikes on Russian oil refineries, fuel depots, and other strategic targets in an effort to reduce Moscow's energy revenues and increase economic pressure.
The overnight drone assault on Sept. 13 brought the war close to Poland's border, with strikes reported in Volyn Oblast in northwestern Ukraine near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk border crossing.
Russian drones damaged a gas station near the crossing and struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train near Ukraine's border with Poland.
At least four Russian strikes on gas stations in Kyiv were recorded over the past week. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Sept. 11 that the city lacks the resources to build shelters at every gas station and is also facing a shortage of weapons needed to intercept Russian drones and missiles.
Russia has previously used drone attacks on gas stations to disrupt fuel supplies and road logistics, particularly in Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. By August, the tactic had spread into central regions, with dozens of gas stations struck over the summer.

articles.title: Kremlin calls Putin-Zelenskyy meeting at G20 summit in Miami "impossible"
articles.body:
Kremlin calls Putin-Zelenskyy meeting at G20 summit in Miami "impossible"
Russian ruler Vladimir Putin has rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's proposal to hold talks on ending the war on the sidelines of the G20 summit in the United States.
Source: Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov in comments to AFP, as reported by France24
Details: In an interview published on Saturday, Zelenskyy said he is ready to travel to the G20 summit in Miami and meet Putin if the Russian ruler also attends the meeting.
However, Peskov immediately rejected such a possibility, calling it "impossible". He stressed that Putin is ready to meet Zelenskyy only in Moscow.
When asked whether the Kremlin is considering an alternative location for a meeting with Zelenskyy, Peskov replied: "There is a readiness to meet him in Moscow."
There is currently no official confirmation that Putin will attend the G20 summit in December.
For his part, Zelenskyy said in a conversation with German journalists that if both leaders were invited to the summit, he would be ready for talks.
"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions. It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter," the Ukrainian leader said. All that matters are "results", he added.
Assessing Ukraine's position ahead of possible diplomatic contact, Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine is now much stronger on the battlefield than it was last year. That is why the Ukrainian authorities consider the current position favourable for starting negotiations.
For reference: Ukraine has repeatedly proposed in recent years that Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin hold a personal meeting in neutral territory to discuss ending Russia's war against Ukraine. However, Russia has consistently rejected the proposal, offering a meeting only in Moscow.
Background:
- Last weekend, US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv. Washington continues to insist on direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.
- On 12 September, Kushner addressed the annual YES security forum in Kyiv by video link. He said that the only thing missing for an agreement to end the war is Ukraine's consent to give up its territories within the boundaries demanded by Putin.
- The Ukrainian side had previously suggested that negotiations could take place as early as September. However, on 7 September, the Kremlin said that it was "too early" to discuss the location or dates of meetings.
- On 12 September, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov called Russia's invitation for Zelenskyy to visit Moscow "a gesture of goodwill". He also claimed that Russia remains open to talks with Ukraine, but said it would not halt the fighting for the duration of such talks.

articles.title: Kremlin hints at returning to tripartite Ukraine talks in October
articles.body:
The Kremlin said Sunday that three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. on ending Europe's worst conflict since World War II could be held in October, Russian media reported.
"We do not rule out such a possibility; we are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists, according to Russia's Ria Novosti and Tass news agencies.
Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled efforts to end the more than four-year war, with U.S. negotiators visiting Kyiv and Moscow, and U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin speaking by phone.
Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed, while U.S.-led efforts stalled.
In an interview released Saturday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G-20 summit for talks.
But Peskov immediately ruled it out as "impossible," speaking to AFP in New Delhi Saturday, repeating Moscow's demand that a meeting only take place in the Russian capital.
Zelenskyy's chief of staff also said Saturday Ukraine expects talks on a peace settlement to resume next month.
"We are preparing for October," Kyrylo Budanov told journalists, confirming the talks would take place in a three-way format. He did not give a precise date or location for the meetings.
U.S. negotiators visited Moscow and Kyiv last weekend to explore a peaceful resolution to the war in Ukraine. They also discussed the possible resumption of the three-way dialogue, suspended for months.
Negotiators conduct the talks and must consult their heads of state throughout the process. A direct meeting between the presidents of the U.S., Russia and Ukraine is only expected at the end.
The U.S. last mediated in February, during direct talks between Russia and Ukraine in Switzerland. Budanov was part of the Ukrainian delegation at the time.
Putin, however, has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face meeting with Zelenskyy to broker an end to the conflict, which has killed thousands and crippled both countries' economies.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have escalated long-range strikes against each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.
Previous rounds of talks have foundered, with Moscow so far unwilling to drop its demands to end the fighting, including that Ukraine cede territory in the east not captured by Russian troops.
On Sunday, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov told journalists, including AFP, there is so far no "coordinated package" on which to base negotiations.
"Currently, the idea is to agree on the territorial issue. But there are also many other questions," he added.

Lukashenko is preparing to wage war against his own people - intelligence
Kyiv • UNN

articles.title: International Painting Competition Sorena to focus on Minab martyred children
articles.body:
International Painting Competition Sorena to focus on Minab martyred children
TEHRAN – The unveiling ceremony of the poster and the press conference for the International Painting Competition Sorena, with the theme “Iran through the eyes of Iranian children in and abroad, and children around the world,” was held on Sunday at the Islamic Culture and Relations Organization (ICRO) in Tehran.
The competition is being held in collaboration with the Abbas Abad Cultural and Tourism Area, the General Directorate for Cultural and Social Affairs of Iranians Abroad at the ICRO, the Art Bureau of the Islamic Dissemination Organization, and the Kian Iranian Smart Technologies Development Group (iGap messenger). The competition is centered on the children who were martyred at the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, ILNA reported.
At the conference, Seyyed Mohammad Hossein Hejazi, CEO of the Abbas Abad Cultural and Tourism Area; Hojjatoleslam Ali Ahadi, Director General of Cultural and Social Affairs for Iranians Abroad at the ICRO; Hossein Divsalar, Deputy for the Development of Scientific and Cultural Cooperation at the ICRO; Ali Janbaz, CEO of Soureh Omid at the Art Bureau; and Rabiei, Deputy of the iGap messenger, provided explanations regarding various dimensions of this event.
Hojjatoleslam Ahadi stated during the meeting that Iranians living abroad remain a part of Iranian society, and their connection to and presence in the country’s cultural affairs are of great importance.
He added that many of these compatriots live outside Iran’s borders for reasons such as education or employment, and various programs have been planned over the past few years to maintain and strengthen their connection with the country.
Ahadi continued that in recent weeks, the first e-sports league specifically for Iranians abroad has been designed and implemented, and he expressed hope that these initiatives would contribute to honoring Iranian culture and art.
Also speaking at the event, Mohammad Hossein Hejazi said that if the potential of Iranian art, the role of children in the country’s future, as well as the issue of peace and the unequal war against Iran are to be addressed, the children of Minab are a clear example to express this.
For his part, Ali Janbaz emphasized the necessity of registering this event in global memory, stating that this tragedy must be recorded as one of the significant crimes of the United States against humanity.
He added that if such events are not seriously documented and followed up on, the possibility of their repetition remains, and one of the effective factors in globalizing the crime against the children of Minab has been the efforts of Iranians living abroad.
Janbaz continued that one should not remain solely in the stage of mourning when facing this incident; it is necessary to move beyond this stage toward action and movement.
He said that painting, as one of the international languages, can play an important role in making this narrative enduring, and the innocent and oppressed narrative of the Minab children even has the capacity to be pursued in international judicial forums.
Deputy of the iGap messenger Rabiei referred to the capacity of this messenger to cover the Sorena competition, stating that with 30 million installs and seven million active users, iGap can convey the message of this event to a wide range of Iranians inside and outside the country.
Hossein Divsalar continued the meeting by pointing to the role of narrative in shaping historical memory, stating that history is not composed only of a collection of events and occurrences, and in many cases, the way an event is narrated can be more important than the event itself.
“If the narrative of an event is not paid attention to, over time, the positions of the oppressor and the oppressed, the victor and the defeated, may shift, and a different image of reality may be formed,” he added.
Divsalar added that in the Minab case, a significant number of young students were targeted, and this characteristic distinguishes this incident from many other historical examples.
“In incidents such as Hiroshima or the Vietnam War, a large number of women and children lost their lives, but in those cases, women and children were not the sole targets of the attack; whereas in Minab, the children present at the school were directly targeted by the crime,” he noted.
“Iran is not a warmongering country, but it defends itself and its homeland against threats, and possessing defense capabilities is essential for the country,” he asserted.
Emphasizing the importance of soft power, Divsalar said that in today’s conditions, possessing hard power and military capability is very important, but soft power is also considered an important and equal component in the country’s authority.
“Iran possesses a vast and unparalleled cultural heritage, and the important issue is that the capacity of cultural diplomacy, alongside military authority, can present an image of the powerful Iran of today to the world,” he underlined.
He also emphasized that the Sorena event is an important initiative that has taken its name from the martyred child of Minab and can be effective in reflecting part of the US crime against Iranian children at the international level.
The International Painting Competition Sorena has considered cultural and cash prizes for its winners, and the responsibility for judging the works will be with the Art Bureau for Children and Adolescents.
According to the organizers, the selected works will be exhibited in various countries after being judged, and an exhibition of the competition’s entries will also be held at Tabiat Bridge.
At the end of the ceremony, the poster for the event was unveiled.
On February 28, the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan province, became the site of a devastating massacre as the United States and Israel initiated their strikes against Iran.
While dozens of girls and boys aged between 7 and 12 were beginning their lessons, the school was targeted by a missile strike that caused the building to collapse, trapping children and teachers beneath the rubble. Iranian authorities confirmed a final death toll of 168 people, with at least 95 others wounded, marking one of the most harrowing incidents of the conflict's opening day.

articles.title: Suspected Russian spy behind drone attack in Leipzig
articles.body:
Suspected Russian spy behind drone attack in Leipzig
A Belarusian citizen and a Russian national linked to the country’s military intelligence services have been identified as the main suspects in the August drone attack.
German security authorities have identified with a high degree of probability a Belarusian citizen and a Russian national linked to the country’s military intelligence services as the main suspects in the August drone attack on the Leipzig-Halle airport, according to two senior German security officials and confidential documents seen by Welt.
Welt, which like POLITICO is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, has reviewed confidential investigative files that have not previously been made public and spoke with four senior security officials from different federal and state agencies. The officials, like others cited in the article, were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
German agencies involved in the investigation include the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the Federal Criminal Police Office, the Federal Intelligence Service and other German agencies.
Advertisement
Due to suspected links to other sabotage cases in Europe, the German authorities are coordinating with investigators in Lithuania, Poland, Latvia and Finland. They are also in contact with the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation, according to the confidential documents.
Welt is not naming the suspects in line with German privacy law. Based on the evidence against them, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt held Russia responsible for the attack during a joint press conference on Sept. 1. Russia has denied any involvement.
Airport attack
The Leipzig-Halle airport was attacked by an explosive-laden drone on the evening of Aug. 4. The drone was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft and safely defused. Investigators found debris from two additional drones near the airport.
German security authorities believe the Russian suspect to be affiliated with the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence service, and to have been responsible for planning and the logistics of the attack, according to classified documents reviewed by WELT and one of the senior security officials.
The Russian suspect entered Germany via Turkey through the Berlin-Brandenburg Airport. He later departed from the airport bound for Serbia, and is now back in Russia. Investigators were already aware at the time of his entry that the Russian was associated with the GRU. Nevertheless, he was not put under surveillance after his arrival, according to a high-ranking German security official, because the agencies had limited resources and did not expect him to be planning an imminent attack.
The Belarusian suspect entered the Schengen Area, the border-free travel zone encompassing 29 European countries, via Latvia on July 28, about a week before the incident. Authorities believe he is a “disposable agent” — a criminal hired to carry out acts of sabotage. The Russian national is said to have organized the explosives and directed the Belarusian suspect, according to a senior German federal security official.
Advertisement
Some 1.8 kilograms of the explosive Semtex was to be used across all three drones — about 600 grams per drone — according to the high-ranking German security official. The Antonov aircraft, which was the target of the attack, was fueled with approximately 25,000 liters of jet fuel.
Two of the senior security officials, both directly involved in the investigation, said that if the charge had detonated, it would have triggered a massive explosion and destroyed parts of the airport. Previously unseen surveillance camera footage obtained by Welt shows the drone lying right next to the Antonov aircraft. According to authorities, the explosive was concealed inside a food can. The explosion did not occur because a detonator broke off.
One day after the attempted attack, police officers found an antenna structure secured with tape in a tree near the airport. It is believed to have been used to control the drones, according to the confidential documents. On the structure, forensic technicians found remnants of a glove with traces of DNA previously recorded in Finland and Lithuania. The Belarusian suspect has a criminal record in those countries, according to one of the senior security officials (in Finland, for example, he was charged with theft, among other offenses).
The Polish authorities also believe the suspect was involved in a fire at a home improvement store in the city of Łódź in the summer of 2024, according to a senior security official. (The Łódź public prosecutor’s office has likewise classified the incident as sabotage.) German investigators view the fact that he was also involved in the Leipzig attack as further evidence of Russian involvement.
According to the high-ranking German security official, the explosives used in Leipzig were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia. Investigators believe they were transported in hidden compartments in trucks and subsequently cached underground. Police found several possible hiding places near Leipzig airport after analyzing data from a rental car used by the suspects.
The confidential police documents also refer to a concrete slab with two handles that was discovered near a pedestrian bridge south of the airport, in the city of Schkeuditz. Authorities believe it had provided access to a hidden storage site. Shortly thereafter, police found another suspected hideout north of the bridge; both storage sites were empty. Investigators also located a hideout in the city of Merseburg, part of the Halle-Leipzig area. According to the police documents, the Russian suspect may have temporarily stored the explosives there.
Advertisement
An examination of the drone that landed on the airport runway revealed it to be a homemade device made from readily available parts, some of which were manufactured using a 3D printer. The four motors were a Chinese brand that is also sold in Russian online stores specializing in “combat technologies.” The food can filled with Semtex was attached to the drone with a mount, according to the classified police documents.
Alexander Dinger is head of investigations at WELT, a publication owned by Axel Springer, POLITICO’s parent company, He focuses on national security and police investigations. Ibrahim Naber is a foreign correspondent for WELT who has been reporting from Ukrainian frontline regions since 2022. Lennart Pfahler is an investigative reporter at WELT, focusing on national security and extremism.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, The Telegraph, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

In addition, drones reached Nizhnekamsk in the Republic of Tatarstan. On the night of September 12-13, Russia's Unified State System for the Prevention and Elimination of Emergency Situations warned of a UAV attack threat in the republic. Local residents reported hearing explosions, seeing drones flying overhead and air defense systems operating.
Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belyaev said a fire broke out "at one of the city's enterprises" – reportedly the Tatneft refinery.
Several oil-processing enterprises are located in Nizhnekamsk, including Taneco JSC (Tatneft), TAIF-NK JSC, Nizhnekamskneftekhim PJSC and others.
On the night of August 19-20, Ukrainian forces struck the Taneco oil refinery in the Republic of Tatarstan.
